As I hastened along, I crossed a ditch near the Battery and climbed the mound beyond it, where I came upon a man sitting with his back to me, his arms folded, and his head nodding forward in sleep. I thought it would be a pleasant surprise for him if I approached him with his breakfast, so I crept forward softly and touched his shoulder. To my surprise, he leapt up, and it was not the same man I had expected, but another individual altogether. This man wore a similar coarse grey attire, had an iron on his leg, and was lame, hoarse, and cold, just like the first man. However, his face was different, and he wore a distinctive flat, broad-brimmed, low-crowned felt hat. I took in all these details in an instant, for he quickly swore at me, made a weak, clumsy attempt to strike me, and then stumbled into the mist, disappearing from view. 'It's the young man,' I thought to myself, feeling a sudden surge of excitement. I soon found myself at the Battery, where I encountered the original man, hugging himself and limping back and forth, clearly waiting for me. He was terribly cold, and his eyes looked so hungry that I feared he might collapse before my eyes. When I handed him the file, he laid it on the grass, and I thought to myself that he might have tried to eat it if he hadn't seen the bundle of food I had brought. This time, he didn't turn me upside down to get at my belongings, but instead allowed me to open the bundle and empty my pockets while remaining right side up. 'What's in the bottle, boy?' he asked, his voice shaking with cold. 'Brandy,' I replied. He was devouring the mincemeat with great haste, but paused to take a swig of the liquor, his body shivering violently as he struggled to keep the bottle between his teeth. 'I think you have the ague,' I said, concerned. 'I'm inclined to agree with you, boy,' he replied, his teeth chattering. 'It's a bad place around here,' I warned him. 'You've been lying on the marshes, and they're notorious for being aguish and rheumatic.' 'I'll eat my breakfast before I die,' he said, his eyes fixed on the mist surrounding us. 'I'd do that even if I were about to be hanged from that gallows over there. I'll beat the shivers, I'll bet you.' As he ate, he stared distrustfully at the mist, often stopping to listen, his jaws working rapidly as he consumed the food.

Now that I was old enough to be apprenticed to Joe, my sister would interpret his every action as opposition, even something as innocent as Joe sitting with the poker on his knees, raking out the ashes. She would jump up, snatch the poker from his hands, shake him, and put it away. These debates always ended in the same frustrating manner. Suddenly, without warning, my sister would stop talking, yawn, and, as if she had just noticed me, would turn on me, saying, 'That's enough of you! Off to bed with you! You've caused enough trouble for one night, I hope!' As if I had been begging them to bother me. We continued in this way for a long time, and it seemed likely that this pattern would persist when Miss Havisham suddenly stopped walking one day, looked at me with some displeasure, and said, 'You're growing tall, Pip!' I thought it wise to respond with a thoughtful expression, hinting that this might be due to circumstances beyond my control. She said nothing more at the time but later stopped and looked at me again, her expression turning moody. The next day, after our usual exercise, she detained me with a movement of her fingers and asked, 'What's the name of that blacksmith of yours?' 'Joe Gargery, ma'am,' I replied. 'You mean the master you were to be apprenticed to?' 'Yes, Miss Havisham.' 'You should be apprenticed at once. Would Gargery come here with you and bring your indentures, do you think?' I indicated that I had no doubt he would consider it an honour. 'Then let him come,' she said. 'At any particular time, Miss Havisham?' I asked. 'There, there! I know nothing about times. Let him come soon, and come with you.' When I delivered this message to Joe that night, my sister became enraged, asking us if we thought she was a doormat and how we dared to treat her so, and what kind of company we thought she was fit for.

Then, he and my sister would get caught up in these absurd conversations about Miss Havisham, and what she would do with me and for me, that I used to feel an overwhelming urge - quite painfully - to burst into tears, lash out at Pumblechook, and confront him. In these discussions, my sister spoke to me as if she were forcing me to confront some harsh reality at every turn, while Pumblechook, who had taken it upon himself to be my patron, would sit watching me with a disapproving eye, like someone who thought they were wasting their time on me.

In these conversations, Joe didn't say much. But he was often targeted by my sister while they were talking, because she knew he wasn't in favor of me leaving the forge. I was old enough now to start my apprenticeship with Joe, and when Joe sat with the poker on his knees, thoughtfully stirring the ashes, my sister would interpret that innocent action as him opposing her plans, and she would jump on him, take the poker away, and scold him. These debates always ended in the same frustrating way. Suddenly, without warning, my sister would stop talking, yawn, and then turn on me, saying, 'That's enough of you! Go to bed, you've caused enough trouble for one night!' As if I had been begging them to make my life miserable.

We went on like this for a long time, and it seemed like we would keep going on like this forever, when one day Miss Havisham stopped walking, leaned on my shoulder, and said with some annoyance, 'You're getting tall, Pip!' I thought it was best to hint, with a thoughtful look, that this might be due to circumstances beyond my control.

She didn't say anything else at the time, but she kept looking at me, and soon she looked upset and moody. The next day, when our usual walk was over and I had helped her to her dressing table, she stopped me with a gesture of her impatient hand, saying, 'Tell me again the name of that blacksmith of yours.' 'Joe Gargery, ma'am,' I replied. 'You mean the one you're supposed to be apprenticed to?' 'Yes, Miss Havisham.' 'You should start your apprenticeship right away. Do you think Joe would come here with you and bring the contract?' I said I was sure he would be honored to be asked. 'Then let him come,' she said. 'Is there a specific time I should bring him?' I asked. 'Just bring him soon,' she said.

When I got home that night and told Joe about Miss Havisham's message, my sister became furious, more than she had ever been before. She asked me and Joe if we thought she was someone to be walked all over, and how we dared to treat her like that, and what kind of company we thought she was fit for.

Then, my sister and Pumblechook would start talking about Miss Havisham and what she would do for me. They would say such silly things that I would feel like crying and yelling at Pumblechook. My sister would speak to me in a mean way, like she was trying to pull out one of my teeth. Pumblechook would sit there, watching me with a disapproving eye, like he thought he was wasting his time helping me.

Joe didn't join in these conversations, but my sister would often talk to him while they were happening. She thought Joe didn't want me to leave the forge, where I was old enough to start working as an apprentice. When Joe would sit with the poker, thinking and stirring the ashes, my sister would get angry and take the poker away from him. These talks always ended in a frustrating way. My sister would suddenly stop talking, look at me, and say, 'That's enough of you! Go to bed, you've caused enough trouble for one night!' It was like I had asked her to bother me on purpose.

This went on for a long time, and it seemed like it would never change. One day, Miss Havisham and I were walking, and she stopped and said, 'You're getting tall, Pip!' I just looked at her, trying to say that I couldn't help it. She didn't say anything else then, but she kept looking at me with a frown. The next day, when we finished our usual walk, she stopped me and asked, 'What's the name of that blacksmith you're supposed to work with?' I told her it was Joe Gargery. She asked if he would come to her house with me and bring the papers for my apprenticeship. I said I was sure he would be happy to come.

When I got home and told Joe about Miss Havisham's message, my sister got very angry. She asked us if we thought she was someone to be walked all over and how we dared to treat her like that. She wanted to know what kind of company we thought she was fit for.

“Biddy,” I said, after asking her to keep a secret, “I want to be a gentleman.” “Oh, I don’t think that’s a good idea,” she replied. “I don’t think it would work out well for you.” “Biddy,” I said firmly, “I have good reasons for wanting to be a gentleman.” “You know what’s best for you, Pip,” she said, “but don’t you think you’re happier the way you are?” “Biddy,” I exclaimed, getting impatient, “I’m not happy at all with my life. I don’t like my job and I never have since I started. Don’t be silly.” “Was I being silly?” Biddy asked, raising her eyebrows. “I apologize if I was. I just want what’s best for you and for you to be comfortable.” “Then understand this,” I said, “I will never be comfortable or happy unless I can live a very different life from the one I have now.” “That’s too bad,” Biddy said, shaking her head sadly. I had often thought the same thing, and when Biddy said it, I felt like crying because I was so frustrated. I told her she was right, and I knew it was a shame, but it couldn’t be helped. “If I could have been content,” I said to Biddy, pulling at the grass, “if I could have liked my job as much as I did when I was little, things would have been better for me. You, Joe, and I would have had everything we needed. Joe and I might have even become business partners, and who knows, maybe I could have been good enough for you, Biddy.” Biddy sighed and looked out at the ships sailing by. “Yes, I’m not too picky,” she said. It didn’t sound like a compliment, but I knew she meant well. “But instead,” I continued, pulling up more grass, “look at me now. I’m unhappy and uncomfortable. What’s the point of being ordinary if nobody had told me it was bad?” Biddy turned to face me, looking at me more closely than she had at the ships. “That wasn’t a very nice or true thing to say,” she said, looking back at the ships. “Who told you that?” I was taken aback, not knowing where I was going with my thoughts. But I couldn’t back down now, so I answered, “The beautiful young lady at Miss Havisham’s. She’s the most beautiful person I’ve ever seen, and I really like her. I want to be a gentleman because of her.”

“Good. You should try to meet him at his own home. The way will be cleared for you, and you can see his son first, who is in London. When will you come to London?”

I said (glancing at Joe, who stood looking on, motionless), that I supposed I could come right away.

“First,” said Mr. Jaggers, “you should get some new clothes to wear, and they shouldn't be your work clothes. How about this day next week? You'll need some money. Shall I leave you twenty guineas?”

He pulled out a long wallet with complete calmness, counted out the money on the table, and pushed it over to me. This was the first time he had moved his leg from the chair. He sat astride the chair after pushing the money over, swinging his wallet and eyeing Joe.

“Well, Joseph Gargery? You look stunned,” Mr. Jaggers said.

“I am,” said Joe, in a very decisive manner.

“It was understood that you didn't want anything for yourself, remember?” Mr. Jaggers asked.

“It was understood,” said Joe. “And it still is. And it always will be that way.”

“But what,” said Mr. Jaggers, swinging his wallet, “if my instructions were to give you a gift as compensation?”

“As compensation for what?” Joe demanded.

“For the loss of Pip's services,” Mr. Jaggers replied.

Joe put his hand on my shoulder with a gentle touch, like a woman's. I've often thought of him since as being like a powerful machine that can crush something or handle it with care, combining strength with gentleness. “Pip is welcome to go and make his fortune, with all the best wishes,” said Joe. “But if you think money can make up for the loss of the little boy who came to the forge and was like a friend to me, then you're wrong.”

Oh, dear good Joe, whom I was so ready to leave and so ungrateful to, I see you again with your strong blacksmith's arm and your broad chest heaving, and your voice fading away. Oh, dear good faithful tender Joe, I feel the loving tremble of your hand on my arm, as strongly today as if it were the touch of an angel.

But I encouraged Joe at the time. I was lost in thoughts of my future and couldn't think about the past. I begged Joe to be comforted, because we had always been the best of friends, and we always would be. Joe wiped his eyes with his wrist, as if he were trying to hurt himself, but he didn't say another word.

Mr. Jaggers had watched this, looking at Joe like he thought he was foolish and at me like I was in charge of him. When it was over, he said, weighing his wallet in his hand: “Now, Joseph Gargery, I'm warning you, this is your last chance. No half-measures with me. If you want to accept a gift that I've been told to give you, speak up, and you'll get it. If, on the other hand, you mean to say—” But to his great surprise, Joe suddenly turned on him, looking like he was ready to fight.

“Good. You should try to meet him at his own house. The way will be prepared for you, and you can meet his son first, who is in London. When will you come to London?” I looked at Joe, who was standing still, and said I could come right away. “First,” said Mr. Jaggers, “you need new clothes that are not work clothes. Let's say you'll come in a week. You'll need some money. Should I give you twenty guineas?” He took out a long purse and counted out the money on the table, then pushed it towards me. This was the first time he had moved his leg from the chair. He sat on the chair, swinging his purse and looking at Joe. “Well, Joseph Gargery? You look surprised?” “I am!” said Joe, very firmly. “It was understood that you didn't want anything for yourself, remember?” “It was understood,” said Joe. “And it still is. And it always will be.” “But what,” said Mr. Jaggers, swinging his purse, “if I was told to give you a gift as a thank you?” “A thank you for what?” Joe asked. “For losing Pip's help.” Joe put his hand on my shoulder, gently. I've often thought about how strong and gentle he was, like a machine that can crush something or handle it carefully. “Pip is welcome to go and make his fortune, and I'm happy for him,” said Joe. “But if you think money can make up for losing the boy who came to the forge and was like a friend to me, then you're wrong.” Oh, dear Joe, I was so ready to leave him and wasn't thankful enough. I see him again, with his strong arm and broad chest, and his voice fading away. Oh, dear Joe, I feel the loving touch of your hand on my arm, as strongly today as if it were the touch of an angel. But at the time, I tried to comfort Joe. I was too caught up in thinking about my future and couldn't remember the good times we had together. I asked Joe to be comforted, because we had always been friends and would always be friends. Joe wiped his eyes with his arm, but didn't say anything else. Mr. Jaggers had been watching us, and it seemed like he thought Joe was simple-minded and I was taking care of him. When it was over, he said, holding his purse: “Now, Joseph Gargery, this is your last chance. I won't accept any excuses. If you want to take a gift from me, say so, and you'll get it. If not, then—” But before he could finish, Joe suddenly turned to him, looking like he was ready to fight.

Mr. Pumblechook stood up again and said, 'I'd like to make a toast to someone special. May I?' I told him it was okay, and we shook hands. Then we drank our wine. I felt the wine go straight to my head. Mr. Pumblechook helped me get some food, giving me the best pieces. He didn't take much for himself. 'You didn't know what would happen to you when you were young,' he said to the food. 'You didn't know you'd be eaten here today.' He got up again and said, 'May I?' I just nodded, and he did it again. I was surprised he didn't hurt himself with my knife. After eating for a bit, Mr. Pumblechook talked about my sister. 'It's sad that she's not well enough to understand the honor of raising you,' he said. I saw him getting ready to make another toast, so I stopped him. 'Let's drink to her health,' I said. Mr. Pumblechook was very impressed. 'That's how you treat people with kindness and respect,' he said. He put down his glass and got up again. 'May I?' he asked. When he finished, he sat down and drank to my sister's health. 'We should forgive her temper,' he said, 'and hope she meant well.' I noticed that Mr. Pumblechook's face was getting red, and I felt my face burning from the wine. I told him I wanted to send my new clothes to his house, and he was thrilled. I explained that I didn't want people in the village to notice me, and he thought it was a great idea. He said he was the only one I could trust. Then he asked if I remembered playing games and going to get me an apprenticeship when we were young. He said he had always been my close friend. Even though I knew it wasn't true, I felt like I had misjudged him, and he seemed like a kind and sensible person.

I discovered that Wemmick was the clerk in the adjacent room. As he stepped out, another clerk was summoned from upstairs to take his place, and I accompanied him into the street after bidding farewell to my guardian. We encountered a new group of people lingering outside, but Wemmick effortlessly navigated through them by stating calmly yet firmly, 'I assure you, it's pointless; he won't engage with any of you,' and we soon cleared a path and continued on our way side by side.

As we walked, I took the opportunity to observe Mr. Wemmick in the daylight. I found him to be a somewhat austere man, slightly below average height, with a wooden face whose features seemed to have been roughly hewn with a blunt instrument. There were a few marks on his face that could have been dimples if the material had been more pliable and the tool more refined, but instead, they appeared as mere indentations. The instrument had attempted to create a few of these decorative touches above his nose but had abandoned the effort without smoothing them out. I surmised that he was a bachelor, given the worn state of his linen, and he seemed to have experienced numerous losses, as evidenced by the multiple mourning rings he wore, in addition to a brooch depicting a lady and a weeping willow beside a tomb with an urn. I also noticed that several rings and seals hung from his watch-chain, as if he were heavily burdened with memories of departed friends. His eyes sparkled - small, sharp, and black - and his lips were thin, wide, and mottled. To the best of my knowledge, he had possessed these features for forty to fifty years.

'Had you never been to London before?' Mr. Wemmick inquired of me.

'No,' I replied.

'I, too, was once new to this city,' said Mr. Wemmick. 'It's strange to think about now.'

'Are you well acquainted with London now?' I asked.

'Oh, yes,' said Mr. Wemmick. 'I'm familiar with its ways.'

'Is it a particularly wicked place?' I asked, more out of a desire to make conversation than to gain insight.

'You can be deceived, robbed, or murdered in London,' he said. 'However, there are plenty of people elsewhere who would do the same to you.'

'If there's ill will between you and them,' I added, attempting to soften the statement.

'Oh, I don't know about ill will,' Mr. Wemmick responded. 'There isn't much of that about. They'll do it if there's something to be gained.'

'That makes it worse,' I said.

'Do you think so?' Mr. Wemmick replied. 'I'd say it's much the same.'

He wore his hat at the back of his head and gazed straight ahead, walking with a self-assured air as if nothing in the streets warranted his attention. His mouth seemed to be perpetually frozen in a mechanical smile, giving him a somewhat artificial appearance. We had reached the top of Holborn Hill before I realized that this was merely a facade, and he wasn't actually smiling at all.

'Do you know where Mr. Matthew Pocket resides?' I asked Mr. Wemmick.

'Yes,' he replied, nodding in a particular direction. 'He lives in Hammersmith, to the west of London.'

'Is that far?'

I found out that Wemmick was the clerk in the next room. Another clerk came down from upstairs to replace him while he was out, and I went with Wemmick into the street after saying goodbye to my guardian. There were new people waiting outside, but Wemmick pushed through them by saying, 'I'm telling you, it's no use. He won't talk to any of you.' We quickly got away from them and walked side by side.

As we walked, I looked at Wemmick in the daylight and saw that he was a thin, short man with a square face that looked like it was carved out of wood. His face had some marks that might have been dimples if they were smoother, but they just looked like dents. He seemed like a bachelor because his clothes were worn out, and he wore several rings and a brooch that showed he had lost many loved ones. I also noticed that he had many rings and seals on his watch chain, like he was carrying memories of his friends who had passed away. His eyes were small, sharp, and black, and his lips were thin and spotted. He had probably had those features for 40 to 50 years.

'Were you never in London before?' Wemmick asked me.

'No,' I replied.

'I was new here once,' said Wemmick. 'It's funny to think about now.'

'You know London well now?' I asked.

'Yes,' said Wemmick. 'I know how it works.'

'Is London a very bad place?' I asked, just to say something.

'You can get cheated, robbed, or murdered in London,' Wemmick said. 'But there are people everywhere who will do those things to you if they can gain from it.'

'If there's a grudge between you and them,' I added, trying to soften what he said.

'I don't know about grudges,' Wemmick said. 'There aren't many grudges. People will do bad things if they can benefit from them.'

'That makes it worse,' I said.

'Do you think so?' Wemmick asked. 'I think it's about the same.'

He wore his hat at the back of his head and looked straight ahead, walking in a way that showed he didn't care about anything around him. His mouth seemed to be smiling, but it was just a habit. We had walked up Holborn Hill before I realized he wasn't actually smiling.

'Do you know where Mr. Matthew Pocket lives?' I asked Wemmick.

'Yes,' he said, nodding in a direction. 'He lives in Hammersmith, west of London.'

'Is that far?' I asked.

Also to Ceylon, particularly for the purpose of obtaining elephants' tusks, he said. I remarked that he would require a considerable number of ships. 'A perfect fleet,' he replied. I was overwhelmed by the grandeur of these plans and asked him where the ships he intended to insure currently traded. He replied that he had not yet begun insuring, but was rather observing his surroundings. This pursuit seemed more suited to his current circumstances at Barnard's Inn. I expressed my conviction, saying, 'Ah-h!' He confirmed, 'Yes, I am in a counting-house, and I am looking about me.' I inquired whether being in a counting-house was profitable. He asked if I meant for the young man in his position, and I replied that I did. He said, 'Why, no; not directly profitable to me.' He spoke as if carefully calculating and balancing his finances. 'It doesn't pay me anything, and I have to support myself.' This did not appear to be a lucrative situation, and I shook my head, implying that it would be challenging to save much from such a source of income. Herbert Pocket said, 'But the key is to look about you. That's the essential thing. You are in a counting-house, and you observe your surroundings.' It seemed to me that one could not be outside a counting-house and still look about, but I deferred to his experience. He continued, 'Then the opportunity arises, and you seize it, making your capital. Once you have made your capital, you have nothing to do but invest it.' This approach was reminiscent of his conduct in our previous encounter in the garden. His manner of coping with poverty was similar to his demeanor after that defeat. He seemed to accept all difficulties with the same air as he had accepted mine. It was evident that he had only the simplest necessities around him, as everything I noticed had been sent from the coffee-house or elsewhere on my account. Despite having already imagined his fortune, he was unassuming and did not appear pompous, which I appreciated. This humility was a pleasant addition to his naturally pleasant nature, and we got along famously. In the evening, we took a walk in the streets and attended the theatre at half-price. The next day, we went to church at Westminster Abbey and strolled in the Parks, where I wondered who shoed all the horses and wished Joe was there. It had been many months since I left Joe and Biddy, and the distance between us seemed vast. The idea of attending our old church in my old clothes on the previous Sunday seemed like an impossibility, both geographically and socially. Yet, in the crowded and brightly lit London streets, I felt a pang of guilt for having left the old kitchen at home so far behind. In the still of the night, the footsteps of the inept porter at Barnard's Inn echoed hollowly in my heart.

He also planned to trade with Ceylon, especially for elephant tusks. I said, 'You'll need a lot of ships for that.' He replied, 'A whole fleet.' I was amazed by the scale of his plans and asked where the ships he insured mostly traded to at the moment. He said, 'I haven't started insuring yet, I'm just looking around.' This seemed more like something you'd do at Barnard's Inn. I said, 'I see,' and he explained that he was working in a counting-house, looking for opportunities. I asked if working in a counting-house was profitable. He replied, 'Do you mean for the young person working there?' I said, 'Yes, for you.' He thought for a moment and said, 'Not really. It doesn't pay me directly, and I have to support myself.' This didn't sound very profitable, and I shook my head, thinking it would be hard to save money from a job like that. Herbert said, 'The important thing is to look for opportunities. You're in a counting-house, so you look around and wait for the right moment to act.' It seemed strange to me that you couldn't look for opportunities outside of a counting-house, but I didn't say anything. Herbert continued, 'When you see your chance, you take it and make your money. Then you can invest it and you're set.' This was similar to how he had handled our fight in the garden. He was very calm and composed, even when talking about his difficult financial situation. It was clear that he didn't have much money, as everything in his room had been borrowed from the coffee-house or somewhere else. Despite this, he had already imagined himself as a successful person and wasn't arrogant about it. I was grateful for his humility, and we got along well. In the evening, we went for a walk and saw a play at the theater. The next day, we went to church at Westminster Abbey and walked in the park. I wondered who took care of all the horses in the park and wished Joe was there to do it. It had been many months since I left Joe and Biddy. The distance between us seemed huge, and it felt like a different world. I couldn't believe I had been away from my old home for so long. The crowded streets of London were overwhelming, and the bright lights made me feel guilty for leaving my old life behind. At night, the sound of the porter walking around Barnard's Inn made me feel empty and nostalgic.

I inquired about the number of clerks, and he replied that they didn't often encounter many, as there was only one Jaggers, and people preferred to deal with him directly. He mentioned that there were only four of them in total. He offered to show me the others, saying I was one of them, in a manner of speaking. I accepted his offer. After Mr. Wemmick had finished putting away the biscuits and paid me from a cash-box in a safe - the key to which he kept hidden down his back and produced from his coat-collar - we went upstairs. The house was dimly lit and shabby, with greasy marks on the staircase that seemed to have been left by people shuffling up and down for years. On the first floor, a clerk who resembled a cross between a publican and a rat-catcher - a large, pale, puffed man - was engaged with several people of unkempt appearance, treating them brusquely, much like everyone else who contributed to Mr. Jaggers's business. As we passed by, Mr. Wemmick commented that the clerk was gathering evidence for a trial at the Bailey. In the room above, a small, flabby clerk with unkempt hair was similarly occupied with a man who had weak eyes. Mr. Wemmick introduced him to me as a smelter who was always ready to melt down anything I might need, and who appeared to be in a state of excessive nervousness, as if he had been experimenting on himself. In a back room, a man with a face-ache, dressed in old black clothes that looked like they had been waxed, was hunched over his work, making fair copies of notes for Mr. Jaggers's use. This was the entirety of the establishment. When we returned downstairs, Wemmick led me to my guardian's room and said, 'You've seen this room before.' I noticed the two repulsive casts with a twitchy leer on them again and asked, 'Whose likenesses are these?' Wemmick got up on a chair, blew the dust off the heads, and brought them down, saying, 'These are two of our most famous clients, who brought us a great deal of credit. This one murdered his master, and considering he wasn't experienced in such matters, he didn't plan it poorly.' I recoiled from the cast, and Wemmick spat on the eyebrow and rubbed it with his sleeve. I asked if the cast was a good likeness, and Wemmick replied that it was made in Newgate directly after the man was taken down. He affectionately addressed the cast, saying, 'You had a particular fondness for me, didn't you, Old Artful?' and explained that he had a brooch made with a lady and a weeping willow at a tomb, which the man had given him. I asked if the lady on the brooch was someone significant, and Wemmick replied that she was just a symbol of the man's game, saying, 'You enjoyed your bit of game, didn't you?'

Then I asked how many clerks worked there. Mr. Wemmick replied that there were only four of them, including himself, because people didn't want to deal with anyone other than Mr. Jaggers directly. He offered to show me the other clerks, saying I was one of them now. After Mr. Wemmick finished putting away the biscuits and paid me from a safe, we went upstairs. The house was old and worn out, with a staircase that seemed to have been used a lot. On the first floor, we saw a clerk who looked like a mix of a bartender and a pest control worker. He was dealing with some shabby-looking people, treating them roughly, like everyone who did business with Mr. Jaggers. Mr. Wemmick said they were gathering evidence for a court case. In the next room, we saw another clerk, a small, flabby man with long hair, who was working with a man with weak eyes. Mr. Wemmick introduced him as a metalworker who could melt anything I wanted. This man was sweating a lot, as if he had been working hard. In a back room, there was a man with a headache, dressed in old black clothes, who was making copies of notes for Mr. Jaggers. This was the entire staff. When we went back downstairs, Mr. Wemmick took me to my guardian's room and said I had already seen it. I noticed the two ugly masks on the shelf again and asked whose faces they were. Mr. Wemmick got up on a chair, dusted them off, and said they were famous clients who had brought Mr. Jaggers a lot of credit. One of them had murdered his boss, and considering he wasn't experienced, he had planned it pretty well. I asked if the mask looked like him, and Mr. Wemmick said it was a perfect likeness, made in prison after he was caught. Mr. Wemmick even talked to the mask, calling it 'Old Artful,' and explained that he had a special brooch made with a picture of a lady and a tree. I asked if the lady was someone important, and Mr. Wemmick said no, she was just a symbol of the man's crimes.

Who is the Spider, I was asked. 'The spider?' I repeated. 'The one with the blotchy, sprawly, sulky appearance,' my questioner elaborated. I identified him as Bentley Drummle, distinguishing him from Startop, who had a more delicate face. However, my companion showed no interest in Startop, instead focusing on Drummle. 'That's his name, is it?' he said, 'I rather like the look of him.' He then proceeded to engage Drummle in conversation, undeterred by the latter's reserved responses. As I watched the two of them, the housekeeper appeared with the first course, interrupting my observation. She was a woman of around forty, with a slender yet agile figure, extremely pale complexion, and a mass of hair that fell in loose locks. Her eyes seemed faded, and her lips were parted, giving her an air of panting. Her face wore an expression of sudden alarm, as if she had been startled. This reminded me of the witches' faces I had seen in a recent production of Macbeth, which had risen out of a cauldron amidst fiery vapors. The housekeeper set the dish down, touched my guardian's arm to signal that dinner was ready, and then disappeared from view. We took our seats at the table, with my guardian placing Drummle on one side of him and Startop on the other. The housekeeper had prepared an exquisite dish of fish, followed by a joint of mutton and a choice bird, all accompanied by an array of fine sauces and wines. Our host served these from a dumb-waiter, carefully replenishing the table with each course. The housekeeper was the only attendant, and she alone set out each dish. I couldn't help but notice her face, which seemed to haunt me like a vision from the witches' cauldron. Years later, I would inadvertently recreate this image by having someone with flowing hair pass behind a bowl of flaming spirits in a dark room. Since then, changes have been made to that part of the Temple, and it no longer has the same isolated feel it had back then, nor is it as exposed to the river. When evaluating an author's merit and determining their place among our most revered figures, we are entitled to assess them from our own perspective and measure them against our own standards. However, in evaluating the power displayed in their works, we must consider their own intentions and compare their creations to their ideal, noting what is lacking. We differ from Mr. Poe in our views on the objectives of art, as he believes the primary goal is to create Beauty, although our disagreement may stem from differing definitions of this term. Nonetheless, in our discussion of his writings, we will adhere to his own standards. The realm of the god of song is accessible from all sides, and there is ample space for all who bring offerings or seek guidance. In his stories, Mr. Poe has chosen to demonstrate his skill primarily in the realm that lies between the boundaries of probability and the realm of superstition and unreality. He possesses a rare combination of faculties, blending the ability to influence the reader's mind with the subtle suggestions of mystery and a meticulous attention to detail that overlooks nothing. Both of these qualities are, in fact, natural consequences of the dominant characteristic of his mind, which is analysis. This analytical mind enables the artist to focus on the intended effect, making all elements subordinate to the central goal. Even his mysterious elements are subject to mathematical precision in his own mind, where the unknown quantity is always known. When he creates a picture, he is aware of the chemical properties of all the colors he uses, and although some of his figures may seem vague or formless, their outlines are as clear to him as a geometric diagram. This is why Mr. Poe has no affinity for Mysticism, which immerses itself in mystery and allows it to permeate all thoughts. In contrast, Mr. Poe approaches his subject from the outside, analyzing, dissecting, and observing with a serene eye the intricate mechanisms at work. This analytical tendency balances his poetic inclinations, granting him the patience to be meticulous and infuse his most fanciful creations with a sense of reality. I feared that my friend's prolonged exposure to misfortune might have finally taken a toll on his sanity. Without hesitation, I decided to accompany the negro to our destination. Upon arriving at the wharf, I noticed a newly purchased scythe and three spades lying in the boat that was to take us on our journey. I turned to Jup and asked, 'What is the purpose of these tools?' He replied, 'Him syfe and spade, massa.' I pressed him for a more detailed explanation, 'Yes, I see that, but why are they here?' Jup responded, 'Him de syfe and de spade what Massa Will sis pon my buying for him in de town, and de debbil's own lot of money I had to gib for 'em.' I was perplexed and asked, 'But what could your "Massa Will" possibly want with scythes and spades?' Jup's response was vague, 'Dat's more dan I know, and debbil take me if I don't b'lieve 'tis more dan he know, too. But it's all cum ob do bug.' Since I couldn't get any clear answers from Jup, whose mind seemed preoccupied with 'de bug,' I boarded the boat and we set sail. With a favorable breeze, we soon arrived at a small cove north of Fort Moultrie. A two-mile walk brought us to the hut, where we arrived around three in the afternoon. Legrand was waiting for us, his eagerness evident in his nervous demeanor, which only served to heighten my concerns about his well-being. His pale complexion and intense gaze further alarmed me. After inquiring about his health, I asked if he had managed to obtain the _scarabæus_ from Lieutenant G——. He replied, his face flushing, 'Oh, yes, I got it from him the next morning. I would never consider parting with that _scarabæus_.' He then added, with a serious tone, 'Jupiter is right about it, you know.' I felt a sense of foreboding and asked, 'In what way?' Legrand's response was astonishing, 'In thinking it's a bug made of real gold.' He spoke with conviction, and I was shocked by his words. He continued, a triumphant smile spreading across his face, 'This bug will be my ticket to reclaiming my family's possessions. It's no wonder I treasure it. Now that Fortune has seen fit to grant it to me, I just need to use it wisely, and I'll uncover the gold it points to.' He called out to Jup, 'Jupiter, bring me that _scarabæus!_' Jup hesitated, 'What, de bug, massa? I'd rather not trouble dat bug – you mus' git him for your own self.' Legrand rose from his seat, his movements grave and deliberate, and retrieved the beetle from a glass case. The _scarabæus_ was a stunning specimen, unknown to naturalists at the time, and thus a valuable find from a scientific perspective. It had two round, black spots near one end of its back and a long one near the other. The scales glistened with a burnished gold appearance, and the insect's weight was remarkable. Considering all these factors, I couldn't help but understand why Jupiter thought it was made of gold, but I was still baffled by Legrand's agreement with this assessment.

I apologize, I had forgotten that Shakespeare won't be popular for another 1,750 years. But doesn't the appearance of Epidaphne justify calling it strange? 'It's well fortified, and owes its strength to both nature and human design.' That's true. 'There are many grand palaces.' Yes, there are. 'And the temples are impressive, comparable to the most famous ones from ancient times.' I agree with that. However, there are also many small, dirty huts and terrible living conditions. We can't help but notice the filth and trash in the streets, and if it weren't for the strong smell of incense, it would be even more unbearable. Have you ever seen streets as narrow as these, or houses as tall? The shadows they cast are so dark. It's a good thing the lamps in the colonnades are kept lit during the day, or it would be like the darkness of Egypt during its worst times. 'This is a strange place! What's the meaning of that unusual building? See, it's taller than all the others and is to the east of what I think is the royal palace.' That's the new Temple of the Sun, who is worshipped in Syria as Elah Gabalah. Later, a famous Roman Emperor will adopt this worship in Rome and take the name Heliogabalus. You might want to see the deity of the temple. You don't need to look up at the sky; the Sun god is inside the building. It's represented as a large stone pillar that ends in a cone shape, symbolizing fire. 'Listen, look! Who are those ridiculous people, half-naked and painted, shouting and gesturing to the crowd?' Some are entertainers, while others are philosophers. Most of them, though, are the king's main courtiers, doing some comedic performance as part of their duties. 'But what's this? The town is full of wild animals! How terrifying! How dangerous!' It's frightening, but not really dangerous. If you look closely, each animal is following its owner quietly. Some are led with ropes, but these are mostly the smaller or more timid animals. The lions, tigers, and leopards are not restrained at all. They've been easily trained to serve their owners like personal attendants. It's true that sometimes nature takes over, and an animal might attack a person or a sacred bull, but such incidents are rare and not worth mentioning in Epidaphne. 'But what's that loud noise? It's even louder than usual for Antioch! It must be something important.'

He had never seen anyone else enter the house, except for the mother and daughter, a porter on occasion, and a doctor about eight or ten times. Several other neighbors testified to the same effect, with no one mentioning any frequent visitors to the house. It was not known if Madame L. and her daughter had any living relatives. The shutters on the front windows were rarely opened, while those at the back were always closed, except for the large room on the fourth floor. The house itself was a good, relatively new building. Isidore Musèt, a gendarme, testified that he was called to the house around three in the morning and found a crowd of twenty or thirty people trying to get in. He eventually forced the gate open with a bayonet, as it was a double gate that was not bolted at the top or bottom. The screams continued until the gate was opened, and then stopped abruptly. The cries seemed to be from someone in extreme agony, loud and prolonged, rather than short and sharp. Isidore led the way upstairs, and upon reaching the first landing, he heard two voices arguing loudly and angrily - one a deep, gruff voice, and the other a much higher, stranger voice.

The mystery of the tragedy in the Rue Morgue remains unsolved. The next day, the newspaper reported that many people had been questioned, but no one had any information that could help explain what happened. The paper printed the important parts of what the witnesses said. Pauline Dubourg, a laundress, had known the two women who were killed for three years. She did their laundry and said they seemed to get along well and were kind to each other. They always paid on time, but she didn't know much about their lives. She thought the older woman might have told fortunes to make money, and people believed she had saved some money. When Pauline went to the house to pick up or drop off laundry, she never met anyone else there, and she was sure they didn't have any servants. The house seemed empty except for the top floor. Pierre Moreau, a tobacconist, had sold tobacco and snuff to the older woman for almost four years. He had lived in the neighborhood his whole life and said the two women had lived in the house for more than six years. They had moved in after the previous tenant, a jeweler, had misused the property. The older woman was a bit childish, and Pierre had seen the daughter only a few times. They kept to themselves and were thought to have some money. Some people believed the older woman told fortunes, but Pierre didn't think so. He had never seen anyone else enter the house except the two women, a porter, and a doctor a few times. Many other neighbors said similar things, and no one knew of any relatives of the two women. The windows at the front of the house were rarely opened, and the ones in the back were always closed, except for one room on the top floor. The house was in good condition and not very old. Isidore Musèt, a police officer, said he was called to the house around 3 am and found a crowd of people trying to get in. He forced the gate open with a bayonet and led the way upstairs. On the first landing, he heard two voices arguing loudly - one was deep and rough, and the other was high-pitched and strange.

The murders in Paris had everyone baffled, and I couldn't see how the killer could be caught. Dupin, however, cautioned against judging the investigation based on its surface level. He believed the Parisian police, despite their reputation for cleverness, often relied on cunning rather than methodical reasoning. Their approach was haphazard, with a focus on short-term gains rather than long-term strategy. While they sometimes achieved surprising results, these were often due to diligence and energy rather than careful planning. When these qualities were insufficient, their plans failed. Vidocq, for example, was a skilled guesser and a persistent individual, but his lack of educated thought led him to make mistakes. He became so focused on the details that he lost sight of the bigger picture. This, Dupin argued, was a common error - being too intense in one's pursuit of knowledge. Truth, he claimed, is often superficial, and the most important knowledge can be found in the broader landscape, rather than in the depths of intense scrutiny. To illustrate this point, Dupin used the example of observing the stars. By glancing at a star indirectly, one can see it more clearly than by staring directly at it. This, he suggested, is because the peripheral vision is more sensitive to faint light. Similarly, in investigation, a more refined and nuanced approach can be more effective than a direct and intense one. Dupin proposed that they conduct their own investigation into the murders, rather than relying on the official inquiry. He suggested that this would not only provide amusement but also allow them to form their own opinion. As he had a personal connection with the Prefect of Police, G——, he was able to obtain the necessary permission to visit the crime scene. They made their way to the Rue Morgue, a dismal street located between the Rue Richelieu and the Rue St. Roch. It was late in the afternoon when they arrived, and the house was easy to find due to the crowd of onlookers gathered across the street, staring at the closed shutters with a mixture of curiosity and morbid fascination.

I had to agree with the rest of Paris that the murders were a complete enigma. I couldn't see any way to track down the killer. 'We shouldn't judge the investigation based on what we've seen so far,' Dupin said. 'The Paris police, who are often praised for their sharp instincts, are clever but that's about it. They don't have a systematic approach, just a lot of flashy tactics that often don't achieve their goals. They make a big show of their efforts, but these efforts are often poorly planned and remind me of someone trying to listen to music more clearly by putting on a robe. Sometimes they get surprising results, but most of the time it's just because they're diligent and active. When that's not enough, their plans fall apart. Vidocq, for example, was good at making educated guesses and persisted in his investigations, but he didn't have a thoughtful approach and often made mistakes because he was too focused on the details. He was so close to the object of his investigation that he lost sight of the bigger picture. There's such a thing as being too obsessed with finding the truth. Truth isn't always hidden; in fact, when it comes to the most important things, I think it's usually right on the surface. The problem is that we often look for it in the wrong places. This kind of mistake is similar to what happens when we try to study the stars. If we glance at a star out of the corner of our eye, we can see it clearly, but if we stare directly at it, it becomes dimmer. This is because our eyes are more sensitive to light when we're not looking directly at something. By being too intense in our pursuit of knowledge, we can actually confuse and weaken our thinking. It's possible to make even the brightest star disappear by staring at it too long. 'As for these murders, let's do some investigating of our own before we form an opinion. It'll be an interesting challenge,' Dupin said. I thought it was an odd way to describe it, but I didn't say anything. 'Besides, Le Bon once did me a favor, and I'm grateful. We'll go check out the scene and see what we can find. I know the Police Prefect, G——, and I'm sure he'll let us take a look.' We got the necessary permission and headed to the Rue Morgue. The street is one of those run-down alleys between the Rue Richelieu and the Rue St. Roch. We arrived late in the afternoon, since it's a long way from where we live. The house was easy to find, since there were still a lot of people standing across the street, staring up at the closed shutters out of curiosity.

I agreed with the people of Paris that the murders were a mystery that couldn't be solved. I didn't see how it would be possible to find the killer. Dupin said, 'We shouldn't judge the investigation by what we see on the surface. The Paris police are clever, but they don't have a systematic approach. They make a big show of their efforts, but often these efforts are not well thought out and don't achieve their goals. Sometimes they get surprising results, but this is usually due to their hard work and activity rather than any clever strategy. When these qualities aren't enough, their plans fail. For example, Vidocq was a good guesser and a persistent man, but he often made mistakes because he focused too much on the details and lost sight of the bigger picture. He was so focused on one thing that he missed the overall truth. This shows that it's possible to be too thorough in an investigation. The truth is not always hidden, but rather it's often right in front of us. I think that the most important knowledge is often the most obvious. The problem is that we often look too hard for the truth and end up missing it. This is like trying to look at a star directly - if you look at it straight on, it can be hard to see, but if you look at it out of the corner of your eye, you can see it more clearly. If we think too much about something, we can confuse ourselves and make it harder to understand. Let's look into the murders ourselves before we decide what to think about them. It will be an interesting challenge, and I also want to help Le Bon, who once did me a favor. We can go to the scene of the crime and see it for ourselves. I know the Prefect of Police, and I can get us permission to visit the house. We got the permission and went to the Rue Morgue, which is a poor street between the Rue Richelieu and the Rue St. Roch. It was late in the afternoon when we arrived, and there were still many people standing outside the house, looking up at the closed shutters with curiosity.

The scent had remained constant, with no break in the chain of events. I had followed the secret to its final conclusion, which was the nail. It appeared identical to the one in the other window, but this similarity was essentially meaningless when considering that the trail ended here. 'There must be something wrong with the nail,' I thought. Upon touching it, the head and about a quarter of an inch of the shank came off in my hand. The rest of the shank was lodged in the gimlet-hole, where it had been broken off. The break was old, with rust covering the edges, and seemed to have been caused by a hammer blow that had partially embedded the head of the nail in the bottom sash. I carefully replaced the head portion in its original position, and the nail appeared whole again - the crack was no longer visible. When I pressed the spring and raised the sash a few inches, the head moved with it, remaining securely in place. After closing the window, the nail seemed perfect once more. The mystery, up to this point, was now solved. The killer had escaped through the window that overlooked the bed. As they left, the window had closed, either on its own or intentionally, and the spring had fastened it, leading the police to mistakenly believe the nail was holding it in place. The next question was how the killer had descended. During our walk around the building, I had already formed an opinion on this matter. About five and a half feet from the window in question, a lightning rod was installed. It would have been impossible for anyone to reach the window from this rod, let alone enter it. However, I noticed that the shutters on the fourth story were of a particular type known as ferrades, which are rarely used today but often found on old mansions in Lyons and Bordeaux. These shutters resemble a regular door, except the lower half is latticed, providing a good grip for the hands. In this case, the shutters were over three and a half feet wide. When we saw them from the back of the house, they were both half open, standing at right angles to the wall. It's likely that the police, like myself, examined the back of the building, but when looking at the ferrades from the side, they may not have noticed their width or failed to consider it properly. As a result, they probably gave this area only a cursory examination, having already convinced themselves that no one could have escaped this way.

The scent had never been lost for a moment. I had followed the secret to its final result, which was a nail. It looked like the other nails in the window, but that didn't matter. What mattered was that this was the end of the trail. I thought, 'There must be something wrong with this nail.' I touched it, and the head came off in my fingers. The rest of the nail was broken off in the hole where it had been. The break was old and had been made by a hammer. I put the head back where it belonged, and the nail looked perfect again. When I opened the window a little, the head stayed in place. I closed the window, and the nail looked whole again. The mystery was starting to make sense. The killer had escaped through the window by the bed. When they left, the window closed by itself or was closed on purpose, and it got stuck because of the spring. The police thought the nail was holding the window shut, so they didn't look any further. The next question was how the killer got down. When we walked around the building, I figured it out. There was a lightning rod about five and a half feet away from the window, but it was too far to reach. I noticed that the shutters on the fourth floor were a special kind called ferrades. They have a lattice bottom and are wide enough to grab onto. When we saw them from the back, they were half open. The police probably looked at them from the side and didn't notice how wide they were, or they didn't think it was important. They probably didn't look closely because they thought no one could have escaped that way.

We don't mean to cause you any harm. I promise you, as a gentleman and a Frenchman, that we don't intend to hurt you. I'm well aware that you're innocent of the atrocities that took place in the Rue Morgue. However, it's not possible to deny that you're somehow involved in them. From what I've already said, you must know that I have access to information about this matter that you couldn't have even imagined. The situation is this: you haven't done anything that you could have avoided, and certainly nothing that would make you guilty. You didn't even take anything when you had the chance to do so without getting caught. You have nothing to hide, and no reason to keep anything secret. On the other hand, you're bound by every principle of honor to tell us everything you know. An innocent person is currently in prison, accused of a crime that you can help us solve by identifying the real perpetrator.

The sailor had regained his composure to a great extent while Dupin was speaking, but his initial confidence was gone.

"So help me God!" he said after a brief pause. "I'll tell you everything I know about this affair, but I don't expect you to believe half of what I say. I'd be a fool if I did. Still, I'm innocent, and I'll come clean even if it kills me."

What he told us was essentially this: he had recently returned from a voyage to the Indian Archipelago. A group he was part of had landed in Borneo and ventured into the interior for a pleasure trip. He and a companion had captured an orangutan. After his companion died, the animal became his sole responsibility. After a lot of trouble caused by the orangutan's aggressive behavior during the return voyage, he finally managed to safely house it at his residence in Paris. To avoid drawing unwanted attention from his neighbors, he kept the animal secluded until it recovered from a foot injury it had sustained on the ship. His ultimate plan was to sell it.

One night, or rather early in the morning of the murder, he returned home from a night out with other sailors and found the orangutan in his bedroom, where it had broken in from a closet where it was supposed to be securely locked. The animal was sitting in front of a mirror, trying to shave itself with a razor, having apparently watched its owner do so through the keyhole. Terrified by the sight of such a dangerous weapon in the hands of a ferocious animal, the man was at a loss for what to do. However, he had experience calming the creature down with a whip, so he used that. As soon as the orangutan saw the whip, it jumped out of the room, down the stairs, and out a window that was unfortunately open, into the street.

The Frenchman followed in desperation; the orangutan, still holding the razor, would occasionally stop and look back at its pursuer, gesturing at him, until the Frenchman was about to catch up.

In the announcement setting forth this reward, a full pardon was promised to any accomplice who came forward as a witness against their fellow accomplices. Additionally, a private notice from a committee of citizens was attached, offering 10,000 francs on top of the amount proposed by the authorities. The total reward was at least 30,000 francs, which is an extraordinary sum considering the victim's humble background and the frequency of such crimes in large cities. No one doubted that the mystery of this murder would be solved immediately. However, despite a few arrests that seemed promising, nothing was uncovered that could implicate the suspected parties, and they were released. Strangely, nearly three weeks had passed since the body was discovered, and no progress had been made in shedding light on the case, before Dupin and I even heard a rumor about the events that had shaken the public. We had been so engrossed in our research that it had been almost a month since either of us had gone out, received a visitor, or glanced at the major news articles in the daily papers. The first news of the murder was brought to us by G, in person. He visited us early in the afternoon of July 13, 18, and stayed until late at night. He was frustrated by his failure to track down the killers. His reputation, he said with a distinctly Parisian flair, was on the line. Even his honor was at stake. The public was watching him, and he was willing to make any sacrifice to solve the mystery. He ended his somewhat amusing speech with a compliment on what he called Dupin's tact and made him a direct and generous offer, which I'm not at liberty to disclose, but it's not relevant to the main story. Dupin politely deflected the compliment but accepted the offer, even though its benefits were conditional. Once this was settled, the Prefect launched into an explanation of his views, interspersing them with lengthy comments on the evidence, which we hadn't seen yet. He spoke at length and, no doubt, knowledgeably, while I occasionally made a suggestion as the night wore on. Dupin sat attentively in his usual armchair, wearing spectacles throughout the conversation. An occasional glance under the green glasses was enough to convince me that he was sleeping soundly, even if silently, during the seven or eight dull hours leading up to the Prefect's departure. The next morning, I obtained a full report of all the evidence from the authorities and collected copies of every newspaper article that had published significant information about the case.

The police announced a reward to help solve a murder case. They promised to pardon anyone involved who came forward to testify against the others. A group of citizens added their own reward of 10,000 francs to the police's offer, making the total reward 30,000 francs. This was a lot of money, especially considering the victim was a poor girl and crimes like this happen often in big cities.

Most people thought the case would be solved quickly. However, even though the police made a few arrests, they didn't find any evidence to prove who was guilty. It wasn't until the third week after the body was found that my friend Dupin and I even heard about the case. We had been too busy with our own research to pay attention to the news. A friend, G, came to visit us on July 13th and told us about the murder. He was frustrated that he couldn't find the killers and felt like his reputation was at stake.

G made a proposal to Dupin, which he accepted. Then G started explaining his thoughts on the case and the evidence they had found. Dupin listened carefully, wearing his glasses and occasionally glancing at G. I made a few suggestions as the night went on. Even though G talked for hours, Dupin stayed focused and attentive.

The next morning, I went to the police station and got a copy of all the evidence they had collected. I also visited the newspaper offices and got copies of every article they had published about the case. This way, we could review everything and try to figure out what had happened.

No one crossed the threshold to discuss the matter in the Rue Pavée St. Andrée, not even with those residing in the same building. M. St. Eustache, Marie's lover and intended husband, who lived with her mother, claimed he was unaware of the discovery of his intended's body until the following morning. It was then that M. Beauvais entered his room and informed him of the news. The reception of this news seemed surprisingly subdued, given its significance. The journal attempted to convey the impression that Marie's relatives were apathetic about her disappearance, which would be inconsistent with the idea that they believed the recovered body to be hers. The journal's insinuations suggested that Marie had left the city with the knowledge of her friends, due to a scandal involving her reputation, and that upon finding a similar-looking corpse, her friends took the opportunity to deceive the public into believing she was dead. However, L'Etoile was too hasty in its accusations. It was proven that the supposed apathy did not exist; the elderly lady was extremely frail and agitated, unable to attend to her duties. St. Eustache, far from being calm, was overcome with grief and behaved frantically, prompting M. Beauvais to ask a friend to take charge of him and prevent him from attending the disinterment examination. Furthermore, despite L'Etoile's claims that the corpse was reburied at public expense, that the family declined a private burial offer, and that no family member attended the ceremony, all these assertions were disproven. In a later issue, the paper attempted to cast suspicion on Beauvais himself. The editor stated that on one occasion, while Madame B—— was visiting Madame Rogêt, M. Beauvais, upon leaving, instructed her not to speak to the expected gendarme until he returned. It seemed that M. Beauvais had taken control of the entire matter, and for some reason, he was determined to be the only one involved in the proceedings, even going so far as to push the male relatives aside in a peculiar manner. He appeared to be strongly opposed to allowing the relatives to see the body. A circumstance that lent some credibility to the suspicion against Beauvais was the discovery, by a visitor to his office a few days before Marie's disappearance, of a rose in the keyhole and the name 'Marie' written on a nearby slate, while Beauvais was absent.

No one crossed the street to investigate. The news of the discovery didn't spread to the other residents of the Rue Pavée St. Andrée, not even to those living in the same building. M. St. Eustache, Marie's fiancé who was boarding at her mother's house, claims he didn't hear about the body being found until the next morning when M. Beauvais came to his room and told him. For such significant news, it's surprising how calmly it was received. The journal tried to create the impression that Marie's relatives were apathetic about the discovery, which didn't fit with the idea that they believed the body was hers. The journal's insinuations suggested that Marie had left the city with her friends' help to avoid a scandal related to her personal life, and that when a similar-looking body was found in the Seine, her friends used the opportunity to make the public think she was dead. However, the journal was too hasty in its accusations. It was proven that there was no such apathy as the journal claimed; the elderly lady was extremely weak and agitated, unable to attend to her duties. St. Eustache was not calm upon receiving the news; he was overcome with grief and acted so frantically that M. Beauvais had to ask a friend to take care of him and prevent him from attending the examination of the body. Additionally, despite the journal's claims that the body was reburied at public expense, that the family declined a private burial offer, and that no family member attended the ceremony, all of these points were later disproven. In a later issue, the journal attempted to shift suspicion to Beauvais himself. The editor wrote, 'Now, a new development emerges. We're told that when Madame B—— was visiting Madame Rogêt, M. Beauvais, on his way out, instructed her not to say anything to the police officer who was expected to arrive, and to let him handle the matter.' It seems that M. Beauvais was trying to control the situation, and for some reason, he wanted to be the only one involved in the proceedings, pushing the male relatives aside in a rather unusual manner. He appeared to be very reluctant to let the relatives see the body. A visitor to his office, a few days before Marie disappeared, noticed a rose in the keyhole of the door and the name 'Marie' written on a slate nearby, which added some credibility to the suspicion against Beauvais.

St. Eustache, Marie's fiancé who lived with her mother, didn't find out until the next morning when M. Beauvais told him. This seems like a very calm reaction to such shocking news. The newspaper tried to make it seem like Marie's family didn't care about her death, which wouldn't make sense if they really thought the body was hers. The paper suggested that Marie had run away from the city because she was in trouble, and that her friends were trying to make people think she was dead by using a similar-looking body found in the Seine. However, this was proven to be false. It was shown that Marie's family was very upset, especially her mother, who was too weak and distressed to take care of anything. M. St. Eustache was also very grief-stricken and had to be taken care of by a friend to prevent him from attending the examination of the body. The newspaper had also claimed that the family didn't attend the reburial ceremony and that they had turned down an offer to pay for a private burial, but these claims were also proven to be false. Later, the newspaper tried to make M. Beauvais look suspicious. They said that he had told a woman named Madame B—— not to talk to the police when they came to the house, and that he seemed to be in control of everything related to the case. They also said that he didn't want the family to see the body. Some people suspected M. Beauvais because a visitor to his office had seen a rose in the keyhole of his door and the name 'Marie' written on a slate a few days before she disappeared.

To me, this article seems to reveal more about the enthusiasm of its writer than anything else. We must remember that newspapers often prioritize creating a stir and making a point over pursuing the truth. The truth is only sought when it aligns with the goal of creating a sensation. An article that simply echoes common opinion, no matter how well-founded, does not impress the masses. The general public tends to regard as insightful only those who propose provocative contradictions to the prevailing idea. In reasoning, just as in literature, it is the clever phrase that is most immediately and widely appreciated, even if it is of relatively low merit. What I am saying is that it is the combination of clever phrasing and dramatic flair in the idea that Marie Rogêt is still alive, rather than any genuine plausibility, that has led L'Etoile to propose it and made it appealing to the public. Let us examine the key points of this journal's argument, trying to clarify the incoherent way it was originally presented. The writer's primary goal is to demonstrate that, given the short time between Marie's disappearance and the discovery of the floating corpse, the corpse cannot be Marie's. The writer's eagerness to minimize this time interval leads to hasty assumptions from the start. The writer claims, 'It is foolish to suppose that the murder, if it occurred, could have been committed quickly enough for the murderers to throw the body into the river before midnight.' We naturally ask, why is this assumption foolish? Why is it unreasonable to think that the murder could have taken place within five minutes of the girl leaving her mother's house, or at any other time of day? There have been murders at all hours. Even if the murder had occurred at any moment between 9 am on Sunday and a quarter before midnight, there would still have been enough time to throw the body into the river before midnight. This assumption essentially means that the murder did not occur on Sunday at all. If we allow L'Etoile to make this assumption, we might as well permit any other liberties. The paragraph that begins 'It is foolish to suppose that the murder...' can be imagined to have originally been thought by its writer as 'It is foolish to suppose that the murder could have been committed soon enough to enable the murderers to throw the body into the river before midnight; it is foolish, we say, to suppose all this and at the same time suppose that the body was not thrown in until after midnight,' a sentence that is inconsequential in itself but not as absurd as the printed version. Were my intention simply to critique this part of L'Etoile's argument, I could safely leave it as it is.

To me, this article seems to prove little beyond the author's enthusiasm. We should keep in mind that, in general, the goal of our newspapers is to create a sensation, to make a point, rather than to advance the cause of truth. The pursuit of truth only happens when it aligns with creating a sensation. An article that simply agrees with popular opinion, no matter how well-founded that opinion may be, doesn't earn any credit with the public. Most people consider someone profound only if they suggest provocative contradictions to the general idea. In both logical reasoning and literature, it's the witty, concise statement that's most immediately and universally appreciated, even though it's often of the lowest order of merit.

What I'm trying to say is that it's the combination of a catchy phrase and a dramatic idea - the notion that Marie Rogêt is still alive - rather than any real plausibility in this idea, that led L'Etoile to suggest it and made it well-received by the public. Let's examine the main points of this journal's argument, trying to avoid the confusion with which it was originally presented.

The writer's first goal is to show that, given the short time between Marie's disappearance and the discovery of the floating corpse, this corpse can't be Marie's. The writer wants to minimize this time interval as much as possible, which becomes an objective in itself. In the rush to achieve this, the writer jumps to assumptions right from the start. 'It's foolish to think,' the writer says, 'that if Marie was murdered, her killers could have done it quickly enough to throw her body into the river before midnight.' We immediately ask, why? Why is it foolish to think that the murder could have happened within five minutes of the girl leaving her mother's house? Why is it foolish to think that the murder could have happened at any given time of day? There have been assassinations at all hours. But if the murder had taken place at any moment between 9 am on Sunday and a quarter to midnight, there would still have been enough time to throw the body into the river before midnight. This assumption essentially means that the murder didn't happen on Sunday at all - and if we let L'Etoile assume this, we might as well let them assume anything. The paragraph starting 'It's foolish to think that the murder, etc.' may have existed in the writer's mind like this: 'It's foolish to think that the murder, if it happened, could have happened quickly enough to allow the killers to throw the body into the river before midnight; it's foolish, we say, to think all this and at the same time assume that the body wasn't thrown in until after midnight' - a sentence that's inconsequential in itself but not as absurd as the one that was printed.

If my goal were simply to criticize this part of L'Etoile's argument, I could safely leave it as it is.

To me, this article doesn't prove much except the writer's enthusiasm. We should remember that newspapers often try to create a sensation rather than tell the truth. Her singing voice was like a rich, flowing cadence, reminiscent of a nightingale's song. When she finished, she handed the guitar to Agatha, who initially hesitated but then played a simple tune, her voice accompanying it in sweet, gentle tones, though unlike the stranger's extraordinary voice. The old man seemed completely enthralled and expressed his gratitude to Agatha, who tried to convey his sentiments to the Arabian woman. As time passed, the atmosphere in the cottage remained peaceful, with the only change being the replacement of sadness with joy on my friends' faces. Safie was always cheerful and happy, and both she and I made rapid progress in learning the language. Within two months, I was able to understand most of the words spoken by my protectors. Meanwhile, the surrounding landscape transformed as the black earth became covered in lush greenery, and the banks were adorned with numerous flowers, their sweet fragrance and beauty a delight to behold. The sun grew warmer, the nights clearer and more balmy, and my nocturnal strolls, though shorter due to the sun's late setting and early rising, brought me immense pleasure. I never ventured out during the day, fearful of encountering the same hostility I had faced in the first village I entered. I dedicated my days to intense study, determined to master the language as quickly as possible. I can confidently say that I improved more rapidly than the Arabian woman, who struggled to understand and conversed in broken accents, whereas I could comprehend and imitate almost every word spoken.

They made many gestures that I didn't understand, but I could see that her presence brought happiness to the cottage, dispelling their sadness like the sun burning off the morning fog. Felix seemed especially happy and welcomed his Arabian friend with big smiles. Agatha, who was always kind, kissed the stranger's hands and pointed to her brother, making signs that seemed to mean he had been sad until she arrived. For a few hours, they all showed joy on their faces, but I didn't get what was causing it. Then I noticed that the stranger was trying to learn their language by repeating words after them, and it occurred to me that I could use the same method to learn too. The stranger picked up about twenty words in the first lesson, and although most of them were words I already knew, I still learned from the others.

As night fell, Agatha and the Arabian went to bed early. When they said their goodbyes, Felix kissed the stranger's hand and said, 'Good night, sweet Safie.' He stayed up late talking to his father, and from how often they mentioned her name, I guessed that their beautiful guest was the topic of conversation. I really wanted to understand what they were saying, so I focused all my attention on it, but it was impossible.

When she finished, she handed the guitar to Agatha, who at first didn't want to take it. The old man was clearly delighted and tried to tell the Arabian woman how much he enjoyed her music, with Agatha helping to translate. From then on, life in the cottage was peaceful again, but this time it was filled with joy instead of sadness. The Arabian woman was always happy, and she and I quickly improved our language skills. The black earth became covered in plants, and the green areas were filled with many flowers that smelled sweet and looked beautiful in the moonlight.
