Safie recounted that her mother, a Christian Arab, had been taken captive and enslaved by the Turks. Due to her beauty, she had captured the heart of Safie's father, who then married her. The young girl spoke highly of her mother, who, having been born free, despised the bondage she was now in. She taught her daughter the principles of her faith and encouraged her to strive for greater intellectual and spiritual independence, which was forbidden to women under Muhammad's teachings. After her mother's death, Safie's mind retained the lessons she had learned, and she felt ill at the thought of returning to Asia and being confined within a harem, limited to childish pursuits that did not suit her temperament, now accustomed to grand ideas and noble aspirations. The prospect of marrying a Christian and staying in a country where women could hold a position in society was captivating to her. The day of the Turk's execution was set, but he escaped from prison the night before and was far from Paris by morning. Felix had obtained passports for his father, sister, and himself, and had previously informed his father of his plan, who then pretended to go on a journey and hid with his daughter in a secluded part of Paris. Felix led the fugitives through France to Lyons and across Mont Cenis to Leghorn, where the merchant intended to wait for a favorable opportunity to enter the Turkish dominions. Safie decided to stay with her father until his departure, during which time the Turk renewed his promise that she would be united with her rescuer. Felix stayed with them, awaiting this event, and in the meantime, he enjoyed the company of the Arabian, who showed him the simplest and most tender affection. They conversed through an interpreter and sometimes through glances, and Safie sang to him the beautiful melodies of her native land. The Turk permitted this closeness and encouraged the young lovers' hopes, while secretly harboring different intentions. He was repulsed by the idea of his daughter marrying a Christian, but he feared Felix's resentment if he appeared unenthusiastic, knowing that he was still at the mercy of his rescuer, who could betray him to the Italian authorities if he chose to. He devised numerous plans to prolong the deception until it was no longer necessary and to secretly take his daughter with him when he left. His plans were aided by news from Paris, which stated that the French government was outraged by the escape of their prisoner and spared no effort to detect and punish his rescuer. Felix's scheme was quickly discovered, and De Lacey and Agatha were imprisoned. When the news reached Felix, it roused him from his pleasant dreams, and he was reminded that his blind and aged father and his gentle sister were languishing in a foul dungeon, while he was free to enjoy the company of the one he loved.

The poor people who came to the door were never turned away. I asked for more than just food or a place to rest - I wanted kindness and understanding. I didn't think I was completely unworthy of these things. As winter approached, I thought about how I could introduce myself to the people who lived in the cottage. I came up with many plans, but the one I decided on was to go into the cottage when the old man was alone. I knew that my appearance was scary to people, but I thought that if I could get the old man to like me, maybe the others would too. One day, when the sun was shining on the leaves outside, the old man's children - Safie, Agatha, and Felix - went for a walk, leaving him alone in the cottage. He picked up his guitar and played some sad but beautiful music. At first, he looked happy, but as he kept playing, he started to look thoughtful and sad. My heart was beating fast - this was my chance to try and make friends with the old man. The servants were gone, and everything was quiet. I took a deep breath and went to the door. I knocked, and the old man said, 'Come in.' I went inside and said, 'I'm sorry to bother you, but I'm a traveler who needs a place to rest. Could I please stay by the fire for a few minutes?' The old man said, 'Come in, and I'll try to help you. But my children are not home, and since I'm blind, it might be hard for me to get you food.' I said, 'Don't worry about food - I have some. I just need warmth and rest.' I sat down, and we were silent for a moment. I knew I had to make the most of this time, but I wasn't sure what to say. The old man spoke up first. 'You sound like you might be from my country,' he said. 'Are you French?' I said, 'No, but I was taught by a French family, and that's the language I understand. I'm on my way to visit some friends who I care about, and I hope they will help me.'

I spent the rest of the day in my hut, consumed by a deep and overwhelming despair. My protectors had left me, and with them, the only connection I had to the world. For the first time, I felt intense anger and hatred, and I didn't try to control these emotions. Instead, I let them take over, focusing my mind on causing harm and destruction. When I thought about my friends, like the gentle De Lacey, the kind Agatha, and the beautiful Arabian, these thoughts faded away, and a wave of tears brought me some comfort. But when I remembered that they had rejected and abandoned me, my anger returned, and I was filled with a rage that I couldn't direct at any human. So, I turned my fury on inanimate objects. As night fell, I gathered various flammable materials around the cottage and, after destroying everything in the garden, I waited impatiently for the moon to set before starting my destruction.

As the night wore on, a strong wind picked up from the woods, quickly clearing the clouds from the sky. The gusts were like a powerful avalanche, and they stirred up a kind of madness in me that broke free from all reason and reflection. I lit a dry tree branch and danced around the cottage with fury, my eyes fixed on the western horizon, where the moon was about to dip below the edge. As the moon disappeared, I waved my torch, and with a loud scream, I set the straw, heath, and bushes I had collected on fire. The wind fueled the flames, and the cottage was quickly engulfed, with the fire clinging to it and licking it with its forked tongues.

As soon as I was sure that nothing could save the cottage, I left the scene and sought refuge in the woods.

Now, with the world ahead of me, where should I go? I decided to flee far from the place of my misfortunes, but as someone hated and despised, every country seemed equally terrifying. Then, I thought of you. I learned from your documents that you were my father, my creator, and who better to turn to than the one who had given me life? From the lessons Felix had taught Safie, I had learned about geography, including the locations of different countries. You had mentioned Geneva as your hometown, and I decided to head in that direction.

But how would I navigate? I knew I had to travel southwest to reach my destination, and the sun was my only guide. I didn't know the names of the towns I would pass through, and I couldn't ask anyone for information. However, I didn't lose hope. My only chance for help was you, even though I felt nothing but hatred towards you. You had given me the ability to perceive and feel, and then you had abandoned me, leaving me to face the scorn and horror of humanity.

I spent the rest of the day in my small hut, feeling completely hopeless and desperate. My friends had left me, and I felt like I had no connection to the world anymore. For the first time, I felt strong feelings of revenge and hatred, and I didn't try to control them. Instead, I let them take over and thought about hurting others. But when I thought about my friends, like De Lacey and Agatha, and the beautiful Arabian, I started to feel a little better. I even cried, which made me feel slightly calmer. However, when I remembered that they had rejected me, my anger came back, and I couldn't direct it at anyone, so I took it out on objects around me. As night fell, I put flammable materials around the cottage and waited for the moon to set before I started my destruction. After destroying the garden, I waited impatiently for the right moment to act.

As the night went on, a strong wind started blowing from the woods, clearing the clouds from the sky. The wind was so fierce that it made me feel like I was losing my mind. I lit a dry branch and danced around the cottage, my eyes fixed on the horizon where the moon was setting. When the moon finally disappeared, I waved my torch and set the straw and bushes on fire. The wind made the fire spread quickly, and the cottage was soon engulfed in flames.

Once I was sure that nothing could be saved, I left the scene and went into the woods to hide. Now, I had to decide where to go. I wanted to get as far away from the place where I had been so unhappy, but I knew that every place would be just as bad for me because I was hated and despised. Then I thought of you, my creator. I had learned from your notes that you were my father, and I thought that you might be able to help me. I had learned some geography from Felix's lessons to Safie, so I knew the general direction I needed to go to get to your hometown of Geneva.

But how was I supposed to find my way? I knew I had to go southwest, and the sun was my only guide. I didn't know the names of the towns I would pass through, and I couldn't ask anyone for help. But I didn't give up. My only hope was that you could help me, even though I felt nothing but hatred towards you. You had given me the ability to think and feel, but then you had abandoned me, leaving me to be ridiculed and feared by everyone.

The creature's actions were a result of her influence, and now it was time for her to face the consequences. Thanks to Felix's lessons and the harsh laws of humans, I had learned how to cause harm. I leaned over her and hid the portrait in a fold of her dress. She moved, and I ran away.

For several days, I stayed near the place where these events happened, sometimes wanting to see you and sometimes deciding to leave the world and its problems behind. Eventually, I wandered into these mountains and have been exploring their vast spaces, driven by a strong passion that only you can satisfy. We cannot part ways until you agree to do what I ask. I am alone and unhappy; people will not associate with me. But someone as ugly and horrible as me would not reject me. My companion must be the same kind of being and have the same flaws. You must create this being for me.

The creature finished speaking and looked at me, waiting for a response. But I was confused and couldn't think clearly enough to understand what it was asking. It continued, 'You must create a female for me, someone I can share feelings with and live a life together. You are the only one who can do this, and I demand it as a right that you cannot refuse.'

The last part of its story had made me angry again, and when it said this, I couldn't hold back my rage anymore. 'I refuse,' I replied. 'No matter what you do to me, I will never agree. You may make me very unhappy, but you will never make me do something that goes against my values. Should I create another being like you, whose combined evil could destroy the world? Leave me alone! I have answered you; you may hurt me, but I will never agree.'

'You are wrong,' the creature replied. 'Instead of threatening me, I want to reason with you. I am mean because I am unhappy. Don't I deserve to be treated with kindness when everyone else hates and avoids me? You, my creator, would destroy me without hesitation. Why should I care about humans when they don't care about me? If I could live with humans in a kind and gentle way, I would be grateful and do good things for them. But that's not possible because humans are afraid of me. I will not give up; I will get revenge for the way I've been treated. If I can't make people love me, I will make them fear me, especially you, my enemy and creator. I swear to hate you forever and work towards your destruction until you regret the day you were born.'

The creature's face was twisted in anger as it spoke, but then it calmed down and continued, 'I meant to reason with you.'

A significant change had taken place in me; my health, which had been declining, was now much improved, and my mood, when not weighed down by the memory of my unhappy promise, had lifted accordingly. My father noticed this change with pleasure and began thinking about how to eliminate the remaining traces of my melancholy, which would still resurface from time to time, casting a dark shadow over the approaching happiness. During these moments, I would seek refuge in complete solitude. I spent entire days alone on the lake in a small boat, watching the clouds and listening to the gentle lapping of the waves, silent and lethargic. However, the fresh air and bright sunshine usually managed to restore me to some degree of calmness, and when I returned, I greeted my friends with a more genuine smile and a more cheerful heart.

After one of these solo outings, my father called me aside and said, 'I'm happy to see, my dear son, that you've started enjoying your old hobbies again and seem to be getting back to yourself. Yet, you still seem unhappy and avoid spending time with us. For a while, I was puzzled about the reason for this, but yesterday an idea occurred to me, and if it's correct, I urge you to be honest about it. Keeping this to yourself would not only be pointless but could also bring triple the misery to all of us.'

I trembled violently at his words, and my father continued, 'I confess, my son, that I've always looked forward to your marriage to our dear Elizabeth as the key to our family's happiness and the comfort of my later years. You two have been close since childhood; you studied together and seemed to have similar personalities and interests. However, human experience can be misleading, and what I thought would bring us together may have actually driven you apart. Perhaps you see Elizabeth as just a sister, without any desire to marry her. Or maybe you've met someone else you love, and feeling obligated to Elizabeth, this inner conflict could be causing the intense pain you seem to be feeling.'

'My dear father, please don't worry,' I replied. 'I love my cousin Elizabeth deeply and sincerely. I've never met anyone who inspires my warmest admiration and affection like she does. My future hopes and dreams are entirely tied to the prospect of us being together.'

'The way you feel about this, my dear Victor, brings me more joy than I've felt in a long time,' my father said. 'If you truly feel this way, we'll definitely be happy, no matter how difficult things seem right now. But it's this sadness that seems to have such a strong hold on you that I want to help you overcome. So, tell me, do you object to getting married soon? We've had some tough times lately, and recent events have disrupted the peaceful life that's suitable for someone of my age and health. You're younger, and I don't think an early marriage would interfere with any future plans you may have for your career or personal growth, considering you have a stable financial situation.'

I had changed a lot; my health was getting better, and my mood was improving too. When I wasn't thinking about my unhappy promise, I felt more positive. My father noticed this change and was happy about it. He wanted to help me get rid of my sadness, which still came back sometimes. When that happened, I would often go to the lake and spend the day alone in a small boat, watching the clouds and listening to the water. The fresh air and sunshine usually helped me feel better, and when I got back, I could smile and be more cheerful with my friends.

After one of these trips, my father called me aside and said, 'I'm glad to see you're enjoying your old hobbies again and seem to be feeling better. But you're still unhappy and don't want to be around us. I've been trying to figure out why, and yesterday I had an idea. If I'm right, please tell me the truth. Not telling me would only make things worse for all of us.'

I started shaking when he said this, and my father continued, 'I've always thought that your marriage to Elizabeth would make our family happy and give me comfort in my old age. You two have been close since you were little, and you seem to be a good match. But maybe what I thought was a good idea has actually caused problems. Maybe you think of Elizabeth as just a sister, or maybe you've met someone else you love. If that's the case, feeling like you have to marry Elizabeth could be making you very unhappy.'

I told my father, 'Don't worry, I love Elizabeth very much. I've never met anyone who makes me feel the way she does. I'm looking forward to marrying her and spending my life with her.'

My father was happy to hear this. He said, 'If you really feel this way, we'll be happy, no matter what's going on right now. But I want to help you get rid of the sadness that's been bothering you. So, tell me, do you have any objections to getting married soon? We've had some tough times lately, and I'm not as young as I used to be. But I don't think getting married would get in the way of your plans for the future, since you have enough money to take care of yourself.'

We visited the tomb of the renowned Hampden and the site where the patriot fell. For a moment, my spirit was lifted from its degrading and miserable fears to contemplate the profound concepts of freedom and self-sacrifice that these sights represented. I momentarily dared to break free from my constraints and look around me with a sense of liberation and a lofty spirit, but the emotional pain had taken its toll, and I sank back into my miserable state, trembling and hopeless.

We left Oxford with regret and headed to Matlock, our next destination. The surrounding countryside resembled the scenery of Switzerland, but on a smaller scale, and the green hills lacked the majestic backdrop of distant white Alps that always accompanied the pine-covered mountains of my homeland. We explored the incredible cave and the small natural history exhibits, where the curiosities were displayed in a similar manner to those in the collections at Servox and Chamounix. When Henry mentioned the latter name, I trembled, and I quickly wanted to leave Matlock, as it was now associated with that horrific scene.

From Derby, we continued our journey north and spent two months in Cumberland and Westmorland. I almost felt like I was back in the Swiss mountains. The remaining patches of snow on the northern sides of the mountains, the lakes, and the rushing rocky streams were all familiar and dear to me. We also made some acquaintances who almost managed to bring me happiness. Clerval's delight was even greater than mine; his mind thrived in the company of talented individuals, and he discovered greater potential within himself than he thought he possessed when he was surrounded by people who were inferior to him. 'I could spend my life here,' he said to me, 'and among these mountains, I would hardly miss Switzerland and the Rhine.'

But he realized that a traveler's life is one that involves a lot of pain amidst its pleasures. A traveler's emotions are always on edge, and when they start to relax, they have to leave the things that bring them joy to experience something new, which in turn captures their attention, only to be abandoned for other novelties.

We had barely visited the various lakes of Cumberland and Westmorland and formed a connection with some of the locals when our scheduled meeting with our Scottish friend approached, and we had to leave. For my part, I wasn't sorry to go. I had neglected my promise for some time, and I feared the consequences of disappointing the demon. He might still be in Switzerland, seeking revenge on my family. This thought haunted me and tormented me at every moment, depriving me of any potential rest and peace. I anxiously awaited my letters, and if they were delayed, I was miserable and overwhelmed by a thousand fears. When the letters arrived, and I saw that they were from Elizabeth or my father, I hardly dared to read them and discover my fate. Sometimes I thought that the monster was following me and might hasten my punishment by killing my companion.

We visited the tomb of the famous Hampden and the field where he died. For a moment, I felt my spirit lift as I thought about the ideas of freedom and sacrifice that these sights represented. I tried to shake off my fears and look around me with a sense of freedom, but my worries soon took over again and I felt hopeless. We left Oxford and went to Matlock, our next stop. The countryside around Matlock looked a bit like Switzerland, but on a smaller scale. The green hills were missing the white Alps that I was used to seeing in my home country. We visited a amazing cave and some natural history exhibits that reminded me of the ones I had seen in Servox and Chamounix. When Henry mentioned Chamounix, I felt a surge of fear and wanted to leave Matlock as soon as possible. From Derby, we traveled north and spent two months in Cumberland and Westmorland. The scenery reminded me of the Swiss mountains, with patches of snow on the northern sides of the mountains, lakes, and rocky streams. We met some people who made me feel almost happy. Clerval was even more delighted, and being around talented people made him realize his own potential. 'I could spend my life here,' he said to me. 'I would hardly miss Switzerland and the Rhine.' But he soon learned that traveling can be painful, even when you're enjoying yourself. You're always on the move, and just when you start to relax, you have to leave and find something new to do. We had just started to like the lakes and the people in Cumberland and Westmorland when it was time to meet our friend from Scotland, so we left. I wasn't sorry to go, because I had been putting off my promise for too long and I was worried about what might happen if I didn't keep it. I was afraid that the monster might take revenge on my family if I didn't do what I said I would do. This thought haunted me and made me anxious all the time. I waited eagerly for letters from home, and if they were late, I was miserable. When they finally arrived, I was too afraid to read them and find out what had happened. Sometimes I thought the monster was following me and might hurt Clerval if I didn't hurry up.

I climbed up the shed and slipped into my window just before dawn broke. My new clothes were all stained with grease and clay, and I was exhausted. 

CHAPTER III.

In the morning, I received a stern lecture from old Miss Watson because of my dirty clothes, but the widow just cleaned off the stains and looked at me with such pity that I thought I'd try to behave for a while. Then Miss Watson took me to the closet to pray, but nothing seemed to come of it. She told me to pray every day and that I'd get whatever I asked for, but that wasn't true. I tried it once and got a fishing line, but no hooks - it was useless without them. I asked for hooks several times, but it never worked out. One day, I asked Miss Watson to try praying for me, but she just called me a fool and wouldn't explain why. 

I sat down in the woods one day, thinking deeply about it. I wondered, if prayer could get you anything, why couldn't Deacon Winn get back the money he lost on pork? Why couldn't the widow get back her stolen silver snuffbox? Why couldn't Miss Watson gain some weight? I decided that there was no point to it. I told the widow about my thoughts, and she said that the only thing you could get from praying was spiritual gifts. She explained that this meant helping others, doing everything I could for them, and always looking out for them, never thinking of myself. This included being kind to Miss Watson, as I understood it. I thought about it for a long time in the woods, but I couldn't see any benefit to it, except for the other people, so I decided to just let it go. Sometimes the widow would talk to me about Providence in a way that made my mouth water, but then Miss Watson would contradict her the next day. I thought I could see that there were two different Providences, and a person would be better off with the widow's, but if Miss Watson's got them, they were doomed. I thought it all through and decided I'd rather follow the widow's, if that's what she wanted, though I couldn't understand how it would make me any better, considering how ignorant and low-down I was.

My father, Pap, had been gone for over a year, which was a relief for me - I didn't want to see him again. He used to beat me whenever he was sober and could catch me, so I'd often run to the woods when he was around. Around that time, his body was found in the river, drowned, about twelve miles upstream from town, or so people said.

I just expected someone would be hiding in it, because people often did that to trick others, and when someone had pulled a small boat out most of the way, they'd jump up and laugh. But that wasn't the case this time. It was definitely a drift canoe, and I climbed in and paddled it to shore. I thought to myself, the old man will be happy when he sees this - it's worth about ten dollars. But when I got to shore, my dad wasn't in sight yet, and as I was pulling the canoe into a small creek lined with vines and willows, I had another idea: I figured I'd hide it well, and instead of running into the woods when I took off, I'd go down the river about fifty miles and set up camp in one place for good, and not have such a tough time walking on foot.

It was pretty close to our shack, and I thought I heard my dad coming all the time, but I managed to hide the canoe; then I went out and looked around a bunch of willows, and there was my dad down the path a ways, taking aim at a bird with his gun. So he hadn't seen anything.

When he came along, I was busy pulling in a fishing line. He scolded me a bit for being so slow, but I told him I fell into the river, and that's what made me so late. I knew he'd see that I was wet, and then he'd start asking questions. We caught five catfish on the lines and headed home.

While we were resting after breakfast, both of us being pretty exhausted, I started thinking that if I could come up with a way to keep my dad and the widow from trying to follow me, it would be more reliable than just relying on luck to get far enough away before they missed me; you see, all sorts of things could happen. Well, I didn't see a way to do it for a while, but then my dad sat up for a minute to drink some water, and he said:

'Next time someone comes snooping around here, you wake me up, got it? That guy wasn't here for any good reason. I would've shot him. Next time you wake me up, you hear?'

Then he lay back down and went to sleep again, but what he had said gave me the idea I needed. I thought to myself, I can make it work now so nobody will think of following me.

Around twelve o'clock, we got up and went along the riverbank. The river was rising pretty quickly, and a lot of driftwood was floating by. After a while, a log raft came by - nine logs tied together. We went out in the skiff and towed it to shore. Then we had dinner. Anyone but my dad would've waited out the day to catch more stuff, but that wasn't his style. Nine logs were enough for one time; he had to head straight to town and sell them. So he locked me in and took the skiff, and started off towing the raft around three thirty. I figured he wouldn't be back that night.

I thought someone might be hiding in the canoe to trick people, but it was really just a drift-canoe. I climbed in and paddled it to shore. I thought my dad would be happy to see it because it was worth ten dollars. But when I got to shore, my dad wasn't there yet. I decided to hide the canoe in a small creek with vines and willows, and then I thought I'd go down the river about fifty miles and camp in one place instead of running away on foot.

The creek was near our shanty, and I thought I heard my dad coming, but I managed to hide the canoe. Then I looked around and saw my dad down the path, getting ready to shoot a bird with his gun. He hadn't seen the canoe. When he came over, I was pretending to work on a fishing line. He scolded me for being slow, but I told him I fell in the river, which was why I was wet. We caught five catfish and went home.

After breakfast, we took a nap because we were both tired. I started thinking about how I could stop my dad and the widow from following me if I ran away. I wanted to make sure they wouldn't come after me. I didn't see a way to do it at first, but then my dad woke up and drank some water. He said, 'Next time someone comes sneaking around here, wake me up. That person wasn't here for any good. I would have shot him.' Then he went back to sleep.

What he said gave me an idea. I thought to myself, 'I can make sure nobody follows me now.' Around noon, we got up and went along the riverbank. The river was rising, and there was a lot of driftwood floating by. Then we saw a log raft with nine logs tied together. We took the skiff and towed it to shore. After we had dinner, my dad decided to take the logs to town to sell them. He locked me in and took the skiff, leaving around 3:30. I thought he wouldn't come back that night.

Something occurred to me. I thought, now I think the widow or the parson or someone prayed that this bread would find me, and it has. So there's no doubt that prayer works, at least when someone like the widow or the parson does it. But it doesn't seem to work for me, and I think it only works for certain people.

I lit my pipe and smoked for a while, then continued watching. The ferry boat was floating with the current, and I thought I'd get a chance to see who was on it when it came by, because it would pass close to where I found the bread. When it got near, I put out my pipe and went to where I found the bread, and lay down behind a log on the bank. I could peek through the log without being seen.

As the boat came closer, I saw that almost everyone in town was on it. There was Pap, Judge Thatcher, Bessie Thatcher, Jo Harper, Tom Sawyer, his Aunt Polly, Sid, Mary, and many others. Everyone was talking about the murder, but the captain interrupted and said, 'Be careful, the current is strong here, and the body might have washed up and gotten stuck in the bushes by the water's edge. I hope that's what happened.'

I didn't want that to happen. Everyone on the boat leaned over the side, looking really closely, but they couldn't see me. Then the captain shouted, 'Stand back!' and the cannon fired right in front of me, making me temporarily deaf and blind from the smoke. I thought I was in trouble, but luckily I wasn't hurt. The boat floated away and disappeared around the island. I could hear the cannon firing every now and then, but it got fainter and eventually stopped. The island is three miles long, and I thought they had reached the end and given up. But they didn't. They turned around and started going up the channel on the other side of the island, firing the cannon occasionally.

When they got to the top of the island, they stopped firing and went to the other shore, heading back to town. I knew I was safe now. No one else would be looking for me. I took my things out of the canoe and set up a camp in the woods. I made a tent out of my blankets to keep my things dry, and I caught a catfish and cooked it for supper. As the sun began to set, I started a fire and ate my meal.

I thought I could land almost anywhere, but it wasn't that easy - the bank was too steep. I was nearly at the foot of the island before I found a suitable spot. I decided to head into the woods, figuring it was pointless to mess with rafts as long as they were moving the lantern around. I had my pipe, some dog-leg tobacco, and matches in my cap, which weren't wet, so I was all set.

And you haven't had any meat or bread to eat this whole time? Why didn't you catch some mud-turkles?

How were you supposed to catch them? You can't sneak up on them and grab them, and it's not like you can hit them with a rock. It's not like you could even try in the daytime without being seen.

That's true, you've had to stay in the woods the whole time. Did you hear them shooting the cannon?

Oh, yes. I knew they were after you. I saw them go by, watching them through the bushes.

Some young birds flew by, going a yard or two at a time and then landing. Jim said it was a sign that it was going to rain. He claimed that when young chickens flew like that, it meant rain, and he figured it was the same with young birds. I was going to catch some, but Jim wouldn't let me. He said it was bad luck. He told me that his father had been very sick once, and someone caught a bird, and his old grandmother said his father would die - and he did.

Jim also said you shouldn't count the things you're going to cook for dinner, or it would bring bad luck. And if you shook the tablecloth after sundown, that was bad luck too. He said that if a man owned a beehive and died, the bees had to be told about it before sunrise the next morning, or they would all get weak and stop working and die. Jim said bees wouldn't sting idiots, but I didn't believe him - I'd tried it before, and they didn't sting me.

I'd heard some of these things before, but not all of them. Jim knew all sorts of signs and superstitions. He claimed he knew almost everything. I pointed out that all the signs seemed to be about bad luck, so I asked him if there weren't any good-luck signs. He said:

There are hardly any, and they're not much use to you anyway. What's the point of knowing when good luck is coming? Do you want to try to avoid it? Well, that's a sign that's actually useful, because it's something that might happen a long time from now. You should stay here for the night. Take off your hat. I said, 'No, I'll rest for a bit and then leave. I'm not afraid of the dark.' She said she wouldn't let me go alone, but her husband would be back in about an hour and a half, and she'd send him with me. Then she started talking about her husband and her family who live up and down the river. She said they used to be better off and might have made a mistake by moving to our town. She kept talking until I was worried that I had made a mistake by coming to her for information. But then she started talking about my dad and the murder, and I was happy to let her keep talking. She told me about how Tom Sawyer and I found the six thousand dollars, but she said it was ten thousand. She talked about my dad and how mean he was, and how I was too. Eventually, she got to the part where I was murdered. I said, 'Who did it? We've heard about what's been going on in Hookerville, but we don't know who killed Huck Finn.' She said, 'I think a lot of people here would like to know who killed him. Some people thought my dad did it himself.' I said, 'No, is that so?' She said, 'Most people thought that at first. He almost got lynched. But then they decided it was probably done by a runaway slave named Jim.' I started to say something, but I stopped myself. I thought it was better to stay quiet. She kept talking and didn't even notice I had tried to say something. She said, 'The slave ran away the same night I was killed. There's a three-hundred-dollar reward for him. And there's a two-hundred-dollar reward for my dad too.' She said my dad came to town the morning after the murder and told everyone about it. He even helped look for the killer on the ferry boat. But then he left, and people wanted to lynch him. The next day, they found out the slave was gone, and they decided he must have done it. So, they blamed it on him. While everyone was talking about it, my dad came back and asked Judge Thatcher for money to search for the slave all over Illinois. The judge gave him some money, and that night, he got drunk with some tough-looking strangers and left with them. He hasn't come back since, and people aren't expecting him to until things calm down a bit. Now, people think he might have killed me and made it look like robbers did it, so he could get my money without having to wait for a long time.

Every night, around ten o'clock, I'd sneak ashore in some small village and buy a little food, like meal or bacon, for ten or fifteen cents; sometimes I'd even snatch a chicken that wasn't roosting too comfortably and take it with me. Pap always said that if you get the chance to take a chicken, you should, because even if you don't want it yourself, you can always find someone who does, and a good deed is never forgotten. Although I never saw Pap turn down a chicken himself, that's what he always said, anyway.

In the mornings, before daylight, I'd slip into cornfields and take a watermelon, or a mushmelon, or a pumpkin, or some fresh corn. Pap claimed it wasn't wrong to borrow things as long as you planned to pay them back someday, but the widow said that was just a nice way of saying stealing, and no respectable person would do it. Jim thought the widow was partly right and Pap was partly right, so he suggested we pick a few things from the list and decide not to borrow them anymore, and that way it wouldn't be wrong to borrow the rest. We spent one whole night discussing it, drifting down the river, trying to decide whether to give up watermelons, cantaloupes, or mushmelons. By dawn, we'd made up our minds and decided to stop taking crabapples and persimmons. We felt better after that, and I was glad we'd made that decision, since crabapples are never any good, and persimmons wouldn't be ripe for a couple of months yet.

Now and then, we'd shoot a bird that got up too early or stayed up too late. All in all, we were living pretty well.

On the fifth night after passing St. Louis, a big storm rolled in after midnight, with a lot of thunder and lightning, and the rain came down in sheets. We huddled in the wigwam and let the raft take care of itself. When the lightning flashed, we could see a long, straight stretch of river ahead, with high, rocky bluffs on both sides. After a while, I said, 'Hey, Jim, look over there!' It was a steamboat that had run aground on a rock. We were drifting straight for it. The lightning showed it to us in perfect detail. The boat was tilted to one side, with part of its upper deck above water, and we could see every little chimney and a chair by the big bell, with an old slouch hat hanging on the back of it, whenever the lightning flashed.

Well, it being the middle of the night, and stormy, and all so mysterious, I felt just like any other boy would when I saw that wreck lying there, so sad and lonely in the middle of the river. I wanted to sneak aboard and snoop around a bit, to see what was there. So I said, 'Let's land on her, Jim.'

But Jim was against it at first. He said, 'I don't want to go fooling around any wreck.'

Every night, I'd sneak ashore around ten o'clock in some small village and buy ten or fifteen cents' worth of food, like meal, bacon, or other stuff. Sometimes I'd grab a chicken that wasn't roosting comfortably and take it with me. Pap always said, 'Take a chicken when you get the chance, because if you don't want it yourself, you can easily find someone who does, and a good deed is never forgotten.' I never saw Pap when he didn't want the chicken himself, but that's what he always said, anyway.

In the mornings, before daylight, I'd slip into cornfields and take a watermelon, a mushmelon, a pumpkin, or some fresh corn. Pap always said it wasn't harmful to borrow things if you planned to pay them back someday. However, the widow said it was just a nice way of saying stealing, and no decent person would do it. Jim thought the widow was partly right and Pap was partly right, so he suggested we pick a few things from the list and decide not to borrow them anymore. Then, he figured it wouldn't be harmful to borrow the rest. We discussed it one night, drifting down the river, trying to decide whether to stop taking watermelons, cantaloupes, or mushmelons. By dawn, we had it all settled and decided to stop taking crabapples and persimmons. We weren't feeling great before that, but now we were comfortable. I was glad about the decision, too, because crabapples are never good, and persimmons wouldn't be ripe for a couple of months yet.

We'd occasionally shoot a bird that got up too early in the morning or didn't go to bed early enough in the evening. Overall, we were living pretty well.

On the fifth night below St. Louis, we had a big storm after midnight, with a lot of thunder and lightning, and the rain poured down in a solid sheet. We stayed in the wigwam and let the raft take care of itself. When the lightning flashed, we could see a straight river ahead and high, rocky bluffs on both sides. I said, 'Hey, Jim, look over there!' It was a steamboat that had run aground on a rock. We were drifting straight towards it. The lightning showed it very clearly. The boat was leaning over, with part of its upper deck above water, and you could see every little chimney and a chair by the big bell, with an old hat hanging on the back of it, when the lightning flashed.

Well, it being late at night and stormy, and all so mysterious, I felt just like any other boy would when I saw that wreck lying there, so mournful and lonely in the middle of the river. I wanted to get on board and sneak around a bit, to see what was there. So I said, 'Let's land on it, Jim.'

But Jim was strongly against it at first. He said, 'I don't want to go fooling around any wreck.'

On the fifth night after passing St. Louis, we had a big storm with a lot of thunder and lightning, and the rain poured down heavily. We stayed in our wigwam and let the raft take care of itself. It was a mysterious and spooky scene, and I felt like any other boy would when I saw the wreck lying there so sadly and alone in the middle of the river. I wanted to get on board and explore a little to see what was there. So I said to Jim, 'Let's land on it.' But Jim was against it at first. He said, 'I don't want to go fooling around on no wreck.'

We set off on the raft after dark. Anyone who still doesn't believe that handling a snake-skin is foolish after all it's done for us will likely change their mind after reading on and seeing what else it did for us. The best place to find canoes is near rafts tied up at the shore, but we didn't see any, so we continued on for over three hours. As the night wore on, it grew gray and somewhat thick, similar to fog, making it difficult to see the river's shape or any distance. It became very late and still, and then a steamboat came upstream. We lit the lantern, thinking they would see it. Boats traveling upstream usually kept their distance from us, following the bars and searching for calm water under the reefs, but on nights like this, they would push right up the channel. We could hear the boat approaching, but didn't see it clearly until it was close. It seemed to be heading straight for us. Often, boats would try to see how close they could get without touching, and sometimes the wheel would bite off a sweep, prompting the pilot to laugh and think himself clever. This boat, however, didn't appear to be veering off. It was large and moving quickly, resembling a black cloud with rows of glow-worms, but then it loomed big and intimidating, with a long row of open furnace doors shining like red-hot teeth, and its massive bows and guards hanging over us. There was a yell, a jingling of bells to stop the engines, a flurry of curses, and a whistle of steam, and as Jim jumped into the water on one side and I on the other, the boat smashed through the raft. I dove, aiming to reach the bottom, as a thirty-foot wheel needed to pass over me, and I wanted to give it plenty of room. I could usually hold my breath for a minute, but this time I stayed under for about a minute and a half. Then I quickly swam to the surface, as I was about to burst. I emerged up to my armpits, blew water out of my nose, and puffed a bit. The current was strong, and the boat started its engines again just ten seconds after stopping, as they didn't care much for raftsmen. Now the boat was churning along up the river, out of sight in the thick weather, although I could still hear it. I called out for Jim about a dozen times, but got no response, so I grabbed a plank that floated by and struck out for the shore, pushing it ahead of me. However, I realized the current was drifting towards the left-hand shore, which meant I was in a crossing, so I changed direction and headed that way.

We left on the raft after dark. If anyone still doesn't think it's a bad idea to handle a snake skin after what happened to us, they will after reading what happened next. We were looking for a place to buy canoes, which is usually near rafts parked on the shore. But we didn't see any, so we kept going for over three hours. The night got foggy and gray, making it hard to see the river or any distance. It was very late and quiet when a steamboat came up the river. We turned on the lantern, hoping they would see it. Usually, boats going upstream don't come close to us, but on nights like this, they go right up the middle of the river. We could hear the boat coming, but we didn't see it well until it was close. It was heading straight for us. Sometimes boats do this to see how close they can get without hitting us. This boat was big and moving fast, with rows of lights that looked like glowworms. But then it suddenly appeared even bigger, with its furnace doors open and its front sticking out over us. Someone yelled at us, and the boat's bells rang to stop the engines. There was a lot of cursing and whistling, and Jim jumped into the water on one side while I jumped on the other. The boat smashed right through the raft. I dove down, trying to find the bottom of the river, because the boat's big wheel had to pass over me. I can hold my breath for a minute, but this time I stayed under for a minute and a half. Then I quickly swam back up to the surface, almost out of breath. I popped out of the water up to my armpits, blew out the water, and took a few deep breaths. The current was strong, and the boat started moving again just ten seconds after it stopped. I called out for Jim about a dozen times, but he didn't answer. So I grabbed a plank that was floating near me and started swimming towards the shore, pushing the plank in front of me. But then I realized the current was taking me to the left side of the river, so I changed direction and went that way.

There was a picture of a young woman standing at a window, gazing up at the moon with tears streaming down her face. She was holding an open letter with a black seal and clutching a locket to her mouth. The picture was captioned 'And Art Thou Gone Yes Thou Art Gone Alas.' I thought these pictures were nice, but they always gave me the shivers when I was feeling down. Everyone was sad that the artist had passed away, as she had planned to create many more works like these. You could see from what she had already done what a great loss it was. I figured that, given her temperament, she was probably happier in the graveyard. She was working on what was supposed to be her masterpiece when she fell ill, and she prayed every day and night to be allowed to live long enough to finish it. The picture showed a young woman in a long white dress, standing on the edge of a bridge, ready to jump, with her hair flowing down her back and tears running down her face. She had multiple arms folded across her chest, stretched out in front of her, and reaching up towards the moon - the idea was to decide which set of arms looked best and then erase the rest. However, she died before making up her mind, and now the picture hung over her bed, adorned with flowers on her birthday and hidden behind a curtain at other times. The woman in the picture had a sweet face, but all those arms made her look a bit too strange to me. This young artist used to keep a scrapbook, where she would paste obituaries, accidents, and stories of suffering from the Presbyterian Observer, and then write her own poetry about them. Her poetry was really good. For example, she wrote a poem about a boy named Stephen Dowling Bots who fell down a well and drowned. The poem went like this: ODE TO STEPHEN DOWLING BOTS, DEC’D. It asked if young Stephen had fallen ill and died, and if the people around him were sad and crying. But that wasn't what happened to Stephen Dowling Bots. He didn't die from whooping cough or measles, and he wasn't struck down by unrequited love or stomach troubles. No, his fate was different. He fell down a well, and by the time they pulled him out, it was too late. His spirit had already left this world and gone to a better place.

There was a picture of a young woman looking out a window at the moon, crying. She had a letter in her hand with a black seal on it, and she was holding a locket with a chain against her mouth. Under the picture, it said, 'And Art Thou Gone? Yes, Thou Art Gone, Alas.' I didn't really like these pictures because they always made me feel sad. Everyone was sorry when the artist died because she had planned to make more pictures like these. You could tell from what she had already done that she was very talented. I think she might have been happier in the graveyard, though. She was working on her best picture when she got sick, and she prayed every day to live long enough to finish it. But she didn't get the chance. The picture was of a woman in a white dress, standing on a bridge, ready to jump. She had her hair down and was looking up at the moon with tears on her face. The woman in the picture had her arms folded and stretched out in different ways, and the idea was to decide which way looked best and then erase the other arms. But the artist died before she could finish, so they hung the picture in her room and put flowers on it every year on her birthday. The rest of the time, it was covered with a curtain. The woman in the picture had a nice face, but all the arms made her look a little strange. This young artist used to keep a scrapbook and paste in stories about people who had died or been in accidents from the newspaper. Then she would write her own poems about them. She was a very good poet. She wrote a poem about a boy named Stephen Dowling Bots who fell into a well and drowned. The poem went like this: ODE TO STEPHEN DOWLING BOTS, DEC’D And did young Stephen get sick, and did young Stephen die? And did the people who loved him get very sad, and did they cry? No, that's not what happened to Stephen Dowling Bots. He didn't get sick or die from an illness. He didn't have whooping cough or measles. None of those things happened to him. So listen to what really happened to him, and try to understand. He fell into a well and died. They pulled him out, but it was too late. His spirit had already gone to a better place. They said he was now in a place where good people go when they die.

The following Sunday, we all attended church, which was about three miles away, with everyone riding horseback. The men brought their guns along, just like Buck did, and kept them between their knees or leaned them against the wall. The Shepherdsons did the same thing. The sermon was quite unpleasant, focusing on brotherly love and similar topics that seemed tedious, but everyone praised it as a good sermon. On the way home, they all discussed it, talking about faith, good deeds, and predestination, among other things, which made it seem like one of the most unpleasant Sundays I had experienced.

About an hour after dinner, everyone was dozing off, either in their chairs or in their rooms, and the atmosphere became quite dull. Buck and a dog were lying on the grass in the sun, fast asleep. I went up to my room, thinking I would take a nap as well. As I passed by, I saw Miss Sophia standing in her doorway, which was next to ours. She invited me into her room, closed the door softly, and asked if I liked her. I replied that I did, and then she asked if I would do something for her without telling anyone. I agreed, and she told me she had left her Testament at church, between two other books, and asked if I could sneak out and retrieve it for her without saying anything to anyone. I agreed to do so.

I slipped out and made my way to the church, where I found no one except maybe a few hogs, as there was no lock on the door and hogs like to stay on the puncheon floor during summer because it's cool. It's interesting to note that most people only attend church when they have to, but hogs are different. As I thought to myself, something seemed unusual; it wasn't normal for a girl to be so worried about a Testament. So, I shook it, and a small piece of paper fell out with '_Half-past two_' written on it in pencil. I searched the Testament but couldn't find anything else. The paper didn't make sense to me, so I put it back in the book and headed home.

When I got upstairs, Miss Sophia was waiting for me in her doorway. She pulled me into her room, closed the door, and then looked in the Testament until she found the paper. As soon as she read it, she looked happy, and before I could react, she grabbed me and gave me a squeeze, saying I was the best boy in the world and telling me not to tell anyone. Her face turned red, and her eyes sparkled, making her look very pretty. I was quite surprised, but once I caught my breath, I asked her what the paper meant. She asked if I had read it, and I said no. Then she asked if I could read writing, and I told her I could only read coarse handwriting. She said the paper was just a bookmark to keep her place, and I could go play now.

Jim thought it was ghosts, but I said, 'No way, ghosts wouldn't say, "Dern the dern fog."' As soon as it got dark, we pushed off and let the current take us wherever it wanted. We'd just float, smoke our pipes, and hang our legs over the side of the raft, talking about all sorts of things. We were always naked, day and night, as long as the mosquitoes didn't bother us too much. The new clothes Buck's family had made for me were too nice to be comfortable, and to be honest, I wasn't really into clothes anyway. Sometimes we'd have the whole river to ourselves for hours. You could see the banks and islands across the water, and occasionally a light from a cabin window or a raft. You might even hear someone playing a fiddle or singing. It was amazing to live on a raft. We'd lie on our backs and stare up at the stars, debating whether they were created or just happened to be there. Jim thought they were made, but I thought they just happened. I figured it would have taken too long to make that many. Jim said the moon could have laid them, which seemed kind of reasonable, so I didn't argue. I mean, I've seen a frog lay a lot of eggs, so it's possible. We'd also watch the shooting stars and see them streak across the sky. Jim thought they were stars that had gone bad and got thrown out of the sky. A few times a night, we'd see a steamboat gliding through the darkness, and sometimes it would shoot out a bunch of sparks from its chimneys. The sparks would rain down into the river and look really cool. Then the boat would turn a corner, its lights would disappear, and everything would be quiet again. After a while, the waves from the boat would reach us and rock the raft a bit. For a long time after that, all you'd hear would be frogs or something. After midnight, the people on shore would go to bed, and the shores would be dark for a few hours. We used the lights from the cabin windows as a kind of clock - when we saw the first light of the morning, we'd find a place to hide the raft right away. One morning, just before sunrise, I found a canoe and paddled across a small channel to the main shore. I went about a mile up a creek into the cypress woods to see if I could find some berries. As I was passing a spot where a path crossed the creek, I saw two men running down the path as fast as they could. I thought I was in trouble, figuring they must be after me or Jim.

Jim thought the strange noise was made by spirits, but I disagreed. 'Spirits wouldn't say, 'Dern the dern fog,'' I said. As soon as it got dark, we pushed our raft into the water. When we reached the middle of the river, we let it float freely, and then we lit our pipes and hung our legs over the side of the raft. We talked about all sorts of things, and we were usually naked because our clothes were uncomfortable and the mosquitoes would bite us if we wore them. The new clothes Buck's family had made for me were too nice to be comfortable, and I didn't like wearing clothes anyway. Sometimes we had the whole river to ourselves for a long time. We could see the banks and islands on the other side of the water, and occasionally we'd see a light from a cabin window or a raft. We might even hear someone playing a fiddle or singing. It was great to live on a raft. We'd lie on our backs and look up at the stars, wondering if they were made or just happened to be there. Jim thought they were made, but I thought they just happened. I figured it would take too long to make that many stars. Jim said the moon could have laid them, which seemed possible, so I didn't argue. We'd watch the stars that fell from the sky and see them streak down. Jim thought they'd gotten spoiled and were thrown out of the sky. At night, we'd sometimes see a steamboat passing by in the dark. It would shoot out sparks from its chimneys, and they'd fall into the river, looking really pretty. Then the boat would turn a corner, and its lights would disappear. The waves from the boat would reach us after a while, rocking the raft a bit. After that, it would be quiet again, except for the sounds of frogs or other animals. After midnight, the people on shore would go to bed, and the shores would be dark for a few hours. We used the lights from the cabin windows as a kind of clock. When we saw the first light again, we knew morning was coming, so we'd find a place to hide the raft. One morning, I found a canoe and crossed over to the main shore. I paddled up a small stream among the cypress trees, looking for some berries. As I was passing a place where a path crossed the stream, I saw two men running down the path as fast as they could. I thought I was in trouble, thinking that they might be after me or Jim.

It nearly killed Jim with laughter. He was always the easiest person to make laugh. I took the watch, and Jim lay down and started snoring; eventually, the storm subsided completely, and when the first cabin light appeared, I woke him up, and we hid the raft for the day. After breakfast, the king pulled out an old, worn-out deck of cards, and he and the duke played a game of seven-up for a while, betting five cents per game. When they got tired of it, they decided to come up with a new plan. The duke rummaged through his carpet-bag and pulled out a bunch of small, printed bills, which he read aloud. One of the bills announced that the 'celebrated Dr. Armand de Montalban, of Paris' would be giving a lecture on phrenology at a certain location, with admission costing ten cents, and character charts available for twenty-five cents each. The duke claimed to be this person. Another bill introduced him as the 'world-renowned Shakespearian tragedian, Garrick the Younger, of Drury Lane, London.' Other bills listed various names and accomplishments, including finding water and gold with a divining rod and breaking witch spells. The duke then said, 'But the theater is my true passion. Have you ever acted on stage, Your Majesty?' The king replied that he hadn't. The duke told him, 'You will, then, before you're three days older. The first decent town we come across, we'll rent a hall and perform the sword fight from Richard III and the balcony scene from Romeo and Juliet. What do you think?' The king agreed, saying he was willing to do anything that would pay, but he didn't know much about acting and hadn't seen many plays. The duke assured him it would be easy to learn. The king was eager to start, so the duke began explaining the story of Romeo and Juliet, saying he would play Romeo and the king could play Juliet. The king expressed concern that his appearance might not be suitable for the role, given his age and balding head. The duke dismissed his worries, saying that the audience wouldn't notice, and that costumes would make all the difference. He produced a few old curtain-calico suits, which he claimed were medieval armor, and a long white cotton nightshirt and ruffled nightcap for the king to wear as Juliet. The king was satisfied, so the duke read the parts aloud in a dramatic fashion, acting out the scenes to demonstrate how it should be done. Then, he handed the book to the king and told him to memorize his lines. There was a small town about three miles down the river, and after dinner, the duke said he had figured out a way to travel during the day without putting Jim in danger. He decided to go into town to make the necessary arrangements.

It almost killed Jim laughing. He was the easiest person to make laugh that ever was, anyway. I took the watch, and Jim lay down and snored away. By and by, the storm let up for good, and the first cabin light that showed, I woke him up and we hid the raft for the day. The king got out an old deck of cards after breakfast, and he and the duke played a game called seven-up for a while, betting five cents a game. Then they got tired of it and decided to come up with a new plan. The duke went into his bag and pulled out some printed bills and read them out loud. One bill said that the famous Dr. Armand de Montalban from Paris would give a lecture on the science of phrenology at a certain place on a certain day for ten cents admission, and would also provide character charts for twenty-five cents each. The duke said that was him. In another bill, he was a famous actor named Garrick the Younger from London. In other bills, he had done other amazing things, like finding water and gold with a special stick, and getting rid of witch spells. Then he said, 'But acting is my favorite. Have you ever acted on stage, King?' 'No,' said the king. 'You will, then, before you're three days older,' said the duke. 'The first good town we come to, we'll rent a hall and perform a sword fight from Richard III and a scene from Romeo and Juliet. What do you think?' 'I'm in, as long as it pays,' said the king. 'But I don't know anything about acting, and I've never seen much of it. Can you teach me?' 'Easy,' said the duke. So the duke told him all about Romeo and Juliet, and said he would be Romeo and the king could be Juliet. 'But if Juliet is so young, duke, my bald head and white whiskers will look strange on her,' said the king. 'Don't worry, these country people won't notice,' said the duke. 'Besides, you'll be wearing a costume, and that makes all the difference. Juliet is on a balcony, enjoying the moonlight before bed, and she's wearing a nightgown and a ruffled nightcap.' He pulled out some old suits and a long white nightshirt and nightcap. The king was satisfied, so the duke read the parts out loud in a big, showy way, acting out the scenes to show how it was done. Then he gave the book to the king and told him to memorize his part. There was a small town about three miles down the river, and after dinner, the duke said he had figured out a way to travel in daylight without putting Jim in danger. So he decided to go to the town and take care of it.

The people had moved out of the houses because the bank was collapsing under them. The river was eating away at the land, and sometimes big chunks would fall in. This meant the town had to keep moving back to stay safe. As it got closer to noon, the streets got more and more crowded with wagons and horses. Families brought their lunches from the country and ate them in their wagons. There was a lot of whiskey drinking and I saw three fights. Then someone shouted, 'Here comes old Boggs! He's in from the country for his monthly drunk!' All the people who didn't have jobs looked happy, and I thought they were used to having fun at Boggs' expense. One of them said, 'I wonder who he's going to pick on this time. If he had picked on all the people he's threatened over the years, he'd be famous by now.' Another one said, 'I wish old Boggs would threaten me, because then I'd know I wasn't going to die for a thousand years.' Boggs came riding into town on his horse, yelling and singing like a wild man. He was drunk and swaying in his saddle. He was over fifty years old and had a very red face. Everyone yelled at him and laughed at him, and he yelled back. He said he'd get to them later, but first he had to take care of Colonel Sherburn, who he said he was going to kill. We wish we could wake up to a new world, full of fresh colors and shapes, where the past wouldn't weigh us down. 
Dorian Gray thought that creating new and exciting experiences was one of life's main goals. He looked for new sensations and ideas, even if they didn't entirely fit his nature. He would try them out, satisfy his curiosity, and then move on with a mix of indifference and passion. 
There was a rumor that Dorian was going to join the Catholic Church, and he was indeed drawn to its rituals. The daily mass, with its simple yet powerful elements, fascinated him. He loved to watch the priest perform the ceremony, lifting the veil of the tabernacle or holding up the monstrance with the wafer. He found the ritual beautiful and moving, a symbol of the human story. He enjoyed kneeling on the cold floor, watching the priest in his ornate robes, and feeling the emotion of the moment.

The luxury of the dead was a wondrous thing to read about. He then shifted his focus to embroideries and tapestries, which served as frescoes in the cold rooms of Europe's northern nations. As he delved into the subject, he became completely absorbed, as was his habit, and was nearly saddened by the thought of how time ravaged beautiful things. He, however, had escaped this fate. While summers passed and yellow jonquils bloomed and withered, and nights of horror repeated their shameful stories, he remained unchanged. His face was unmarred by winter, and his bloom was unblemished. In contrast, material things were not so fortunate. What had become of them? Where was the magnificent crocus-colored robe, woven by brown girls for Athena's pleasure, on which the gods had battled the giants? Where was the enormous velarium that Nero had stretched across the Colosseum, with its purple Titan sail depicting the starry sky and Apollo driving a chariot drawn by white, gilt-reined steeds? He yearned to see the intricate table-napkins made for the Priest of the Sun, adorned with all manner of delicacies and dishes for a feast; the mortuary cloth of King Chilperic, with its three hundred golden bees; the fantastical robes that had provoked the Bishop of Pontus, featuring 'lions, panthers, bears, dogs, forests, rocks, hunters - all that a painter can copy from nature'; and the coat worn by Charles of Orleans, with verses from a song embroidered on the sleeves, 'Madame, je suis tout joyeux', with gold thread and pearls forming the musical accompaniment. He read about the room prepared for Queen Joan of Burgundy at the palace in Rheims, decorated with 'thirteen hundred and twenty-one parrots, made in broidery, and blazoned with the king's arms, and five hundred and sixty-one butterflies, whose wings were similarly ornamented with the queen's arms, all worked in gold'. Catherine de Medicis had a mourning-bed made of black velvet, powdered with crescents and suns, with damask curtains featuring leafy wreaths and garlands on a gold and silver ground, and fringed with pearl broideries. Louis XIV had fifteen-foot-high gold-embroidered caryatides in his apartment. The state bed of Sobieski, King of Poland, was made of Smyrna gold brocade, embroidered with turquoises and verses from the Koran, with silver-gilt supports, beautifully chased and adorned with enamelled and jewelled medallions. It had been taken from the Turkish camp before Vienna, and the standard of Mohammed had stood beneath its tremulous gilt canopy. For a whole year, he sought to collect the most exquisite specimens of textile and embroidered work, acquiring delicate Delhi muslins, finely wrought with gold-thread palmates and stitched over with iridescent beetles' wings; the Dacca gauzes, known in the East as 'woven air', 'running water', and 'evening dew' due to their transparency; strange figured cloths from Java; elaborate yellow Chinese hangings; books bound in tawny satins or fair blue silks, wrought with fleurs-de-lis, birds, and images; veils of lacis worked in Hungary point; Sicilian brocades and stiff Spanish velvets; Georgian work, with its gilt coins, and Japanese Foukousas, with their green-toned golds and marvellously plumaged birds.

It was amazing to read about the luxury of the past. Then, Dorian turned his attention to embroidered fabrics and tapestries that decorated the cold rooms of European homes. As he learned more about the subject, he became completely absorbed in it, as he always did. He was almost sad to think about how time could ruin beautiful things. But Dorian himself had not changed. Summer after summer passed, and he remained the same, while material things fell apart. He wondered what had happened to the beautiful robe made by brown girls for Athena, or the huge purple canopy that Nero had put up in the Colosseum. Dorian longed to see the intricate tablecloths made for the Priest of the Sun, the mortuary cloth of King Chilperic with its golden bees, and the fantastic robes that had angered the Bishop of Pontus. He also wanted to see the coat that Charles of Orleans had worn, with its embroidered verses and musical notes made of gold and pearls. He read about the room prepared for Queen Joan of Burgundy, decorated with hundreds of embroidered parrots and butterflies. Catherine de Medicis had a mourning bed made of black velvet with crescents and suns, and Louis XIV had giant gold embroidered statues in his apartment. The state bed of Sobieski, King of Poland, was made of gold brocade with turquoise embroidery and silver gilt supports. For a whole year, Dorian collected the most exquisite examples of textile and embroidered work, including delicate muslins from Delhi, transparent gauzes from Dacca, and elaborate Chinese hangings. He also collected strange figured cloths from Java, books bound in satin or silk, veils from Hungary, and brocades from Sicily and Spain. He was particularly fond of Georgian work with gilt coins and Japanese fabrics with green-toned golds and beautifully decorated birds.

There were people in history whose lives were marked by extreme beauty and extreme sin. One such person was a man who welcomed a royal guest in a lavish tent with decorations and servants dressed as mythological creatures. Another was Ezzelin, who was said to be the son of the devil and had a fascination with death. He was known to gamble with his own soul and had a thirst for blood. Then there was Giambattista Cibo, who took on a false name and had the blood of young men transfused into his veins. Sigismondo Malatesta was a lord who committed terrible crimes, including murder and poisoning, and even built a church to honor his sinful desires. Charles VI was a king who became insane with desire for his brother's wife and could only be calmed by special cards with images of love and death. Lastly, there was Grifonetto Baglioni, a handsome young man who committed many murders, including killing his friends on their wedding day. Despite their evil deeds, there was something fascinating about these people. Dorian Gray couldn't help but think about them, especially at night, and they filled his imagination during the day. The Renaissance was a time when people knew of many creative ways to poison others, but Dorian had been poisoned by a book. He began to see evil as a way to experience beauty. One night, on November 9th, the eve of his 38th birthday, Dorian was walking home from Lord Henry's house, where he had dinner. It was cold and foggy, and he was wrapped in warm clothes. As he turned a corner, he saw a man walking quickly in the mist. The man had a bag in his hand and his coat collar turned up. Dorian recognized the man as Basil Hallward, an artist and friend. But for some reason, Dorian felt a sudden sense of fear and didn't greet him. Instead, he kept walking quickly towards his own house. However, Hallward had seen him and stopped to catch up. Dorian heard Hallward's footsteps behind him and then felt his hand on his arm. 'Dorian, what a coincidence!' Hallward said. 'I've been waiting for you in your library since 9 o'clock. I finally let your servant go to bed and was about to leave when I saw you.'
